data.name: Image Pull Failures
data.desc: The pod can't fetch its container image — ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff. Fails before the container ever runs, so the answer is in Events, not logs.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA — same symptom, 3 different root causes. Always read the Events 'Message' to tell them apart:
  • 'not found'            -> image/tag doesn't exist or is misspelled (fix the tag)
  • 'unauthorized/denied'  -> private image, missing imagePullSecret (add the secret)
  • 'no such host'/timeout -> registry unreachable: network / DNS / firewall

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: Pod is ImagePullBackOff — walk me through it.
A: get pods (see status) -> describe pod (read Events message) -> act on the specific cause. Don't restart blindly.

Q: Difference between ErrImagePull and ImagePullBackOff?
A: ErrImagePull is the first failed attempt; ImagePullBackOff is kubelet backing off and retrying with growing delay after repeated failures.

Q: Private image in Artifact Registry won't pull on GKE — what's wrong?
A: Usually the node service account lacks the Artifact Registry Reader role, OR the pod needs an imagePullSecret. On GKE prefer fixing the node SA IAM.

problems.title: The pod that never comes up
problems.symptom: We deployed the 'web' service to 'drill' 3 minutes ago. It's not serving traffic. The pod is stuck — never reaches Running. Users get nothing.
problems.hint: Look at the pod's Events, not its logs. It fails before the container starts, so no logs exist yet.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> STATUS=ImagePullBackOff (Pending/Waiting). describe pod -> Events: 'docker.io/library/nginx:1.27-alpin: not found'. Registry has no such tag.
problems.rootCause: Deployment references a non-existent image tag nginx:1.27-alpin (missing trailing 'e'; should be 1.27-alpine). Pull returns NotFound, kubelet backs off -> ImagePullBackOff.
problems.fix: Patch the image to the correct tag and let the Deployment roll. Faster + reversible vs re-editing YAML; gives a clean rollout you can 'rollout undo'.
problems.mental: get pods = category of failure; describe (Events) = exact cause; fix targets the cause. This 3-move flow solves Pending, ConfigError, and more.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
# deploy references nginx:1.27-alpin  <-- typo, should be 1.27-alpine

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                        # STATUS = ImagePullBackOff
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=web         # read Events -> exact reason
kubectl get events -n drill --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl set image -n drill deployment/web web=nginx:1.27-alpine
kubectl rollout status -n drill deployment/web
kubectl get pods -n drill                        # 1/1 Running

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Private image, no error until you actually look — missing imagePullSecret
problems.symptom: The 'billing' deployment in drill references an image in a private Artifact Registry repo. The pod never reaches Running. The team lead says 'it worked fine when I pushed the image manually with docker' — so why won't the cluster pull it?
problems.hint: Being able to docker-push an image with YOUR OWN gcloud credentials proves the image exists and that YOU personally have access. It says nothing about whether the cluster — or this specific pod — has been given any credential of its own.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> ImagePullBackOff. describe pod -> Events: 'Failed to pull image ... unauthorized: authentication failed' / 'denied: Permission "artifactregistry.repositories.downloadArtifacts" denied'. gcloud artifacts docker images list confirms the image genuinely exists at that path and tag — this isn't a typo like the earlier drill, it's purely a credentials gap.
problems.rootCause: Neither the node's service account nor the pod has any credential for this private repo — no imagePullSecret is attached, and the node SA was never granted artifactregistry.reader on it. A personal 'docker push' only proves the pusher's own gcloud identity has access; it says nothing about what identity the cluster pulls with at runtime.
problems.fix: Two valid fixes, pick one: (1) grant the node's service account 'roles/artifactregistry.reader' on the repo — the GKE-native approach, nothing to rotate. (2) create a docker-registry imagePullSecret and reference it via imagePullSecrets on the pod/ServiceAccount — works anywhere, but is a credential you now own the lifecycle of.
problems.mental: ImagePullBackOff always splits into the same three buckets: wrong name/tag ('not found'), no permission ('unauthorized'/'denied' — this drill), or can't reach the registry at all (DNS/timeout — the next drill). Read the exact Events text before touching anything; it tells you which bucket you're in.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create deployment billing --image=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/terraform-gke-learning/web-repo/billing:v1 --replicas=1
# no imagePullSecret attached, node SA lacks artifactregistry.reader on web-repo

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                                    # ImagePullBackOff
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=billing                 # Events: unauthorized / permission denied
gcloud artifacts docker images list asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/terraform-gke-learning/web-repo   # confirms the image genuinely exists

commands.label: Fix (IAM route, preferred on GKE)
commands.code:
gcloud artifacts repositories add-iam-policy-binding web-repo --location=asia-south1 \
  --member="serviceAccount:terraform-gke-learning-node-sa@terraform-gke-learning.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/artifactregistry.reader"
kubectl delete pod -n drill -l app=billing        # force a fresh pull attempt
kubectl get pods -n drill                         # 1/1 Running

commands.label: Fix (imagePullSecret route)
commands.code:
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n drill \
  --docker-server=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev --docker-username=_json_key --docker-password="$(cat key.json)"
kubectl patch deployment billing -n drill --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/imagePullSecrets","value":[{"name":"regcred"}]}]'
kubectl rollout status deployment/billing -n drill

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: ImagePullBackOff that has nothing to do with the image — registry unreachable
problems.symptom: The 'reports' deployment in drill can't pull its image. The tag is right, the image is public — nothing about the reference itself looks wrong. describe just shows a pull error that isn't 'not found' and isn't 'unauthorized' — something about a timeout.
problems.hint: Not every ImagePullBackOff is about the image reference or credentials. If the node genuinely can't reach the registry over the network, the error text looks nothing like the other two cases — read exactly what it says before assuming a typo or a permissions gap.
problems.diagnosis: describe pod -> Events: 'Failed to pull image ... failed to resolve reference ... dial tcp: lookup unreachable-registry.internal: no such host'. No 'not found', no 'unauthorized' — a DNS/connectivity failure reaching the registry HOST itself, a third distinct failure signature.
problems.rootCause: The node can't resolve or reach the registry's hostname at all — here, simulated by pointing the image reference at a host that was never real. In actual incidents the identical signature comes from a VPC firewall rule blocking egress to the real registry, a broken Private Google Access setting, or a genuine regional registry outage — none of which are fixable by editing the pod spec.
problems.fix: Confirm the registry hostname is correct and reachable — test from a debug pod on the SAME cluster/VPC, not from your own laptop, since egress can differ between environments. If it's a real firewall/VPC issue, that's fixed at the VPC & Firewall layer (see the GKE Commands tab), not in the Deployment at all.
problems.mental: Read the exact Events wording before diagnosing further: 'not found' (wrong tag), 'unauthorized'/'denied' (credentials), or a DNS/timeout phrase (network can't reach the registry). Same top-level ImagePullBackOff status, three unrelated root causes, three different owners of the actual fix.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create deployment reports --image=unreachable-registry.internal/reports:v1 --replicas=1

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                              # ImagePullBackOff
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=reports           # Events: dial tcp lookup ... no such host
kubectl run netcheck -n drill --image=busybox --restart=Never -it --rm -- nslookup unreachable-registry.internal   # confirm from IN-cluster, not your laptop

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl set image -n drill deployment/reports reports=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/terraform-gke-learning/web-repo/reports:v1
kubectl rollout status -n drill deployment/reports
kubectl get pods -n drill                              # 1/1 Running

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: ImagePullBackOff on a correctly-authorized public image — registry rate limiting
problems.symptom: Several unrelated pods across drill started failing to pull nginx:alpine within the same few minutes — pods that were pulling it fine yesterday. Nothing changed in any manifest. Image name, tag, and credentials are all still correct.
problems.hint: The image, the tag, and the credentials are all fine — so whatever changed isn't the pod spec. It's something about how OFTEN this cluster has pulled from this particular public registry recently.
problems.diagnosis: describe pod -> Events: 'Failed to pull image ... 429 Too Many Requests ... You have reached your pull rate limit'. Matches Docker Hub's anonymous-pull rate limit (100 pulls/6h per IP) — the whole node pool shares one outbound IP, so a burst of pods pulling the same public image (e.g. right after a scale-up) can exhaust it fast.
problems.rootCause: Repeated redeploys/scale events pulling the same public Docker Hub image from the node pool's shared egress IP tripped Docker Hub's anonymous rate limit. Not a permissions or DNS problem — the registry is explicitly refusing further pulls until the window resets, a distinct HTTP status (429) from either 'not found' or 'unauthorized'.
problems.fix: Short-term: wait out the rate-limit window, or set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent so nodes reuse an already-cached layer instead of re-pulling on every restart. Durable fix: mirror the image into your own Artifact Registry repo and pull from there — removes the shared-IP rate limit entirely, and is the standard GKE production pattern regardless.
problems.mental: A 429 in the pull error is its own bucket, separate from 'not found'/'unauthorized'/DNS — the one case where the image reference, credentials, AND network path can all be completely correct and it still fails. This one is genuinely hard to force on demand in a short drill (it's IP+time-window based) — the value here is recognizing the signature in Events instantly the first time you see it for real, not reproducing it live.

commands.label: Setup — hard to force on demand
commands.code:
# Docker Hub's rate limit is per-IP, per-6h-window — not reliably triggerable in a 2-minute drill.
# In practice it shows up after many pods across a node pool pull the same public image in a burst
# (e.g. right after a cluster/node-pool scale-up). Recognize the Events text below instead.

commands.label: Diagnose (what it looks like when it happens for real)
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                    # ImagePullBackOff
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=web      # Events: '429 Too Many Requests ... pull rate limit'

commands.label: Prevention / fix
commands.code:
# reduce redundant pulls:
kubectl patch deployment web -n drill --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"}]'

# durable fix — mirror into your own registry instead of pulling Docker Hub directly:
gcloud artifacts repositories create mirror-repo --repository-format=docker --location=asia-south1
docker pull nginx:alpine
docker tag nginx:alpine asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/terraform-gke-learning/mirror-repo/nginx:alpine
docker push asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/terraform-gke-learning/mirror-repo/nginx:alpine

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

data.name: CrashLoopBackOff & Container Exits
data.desc: The container starts, then exits, and Kubernetes restarts it on a growing backoff. The RESTARTS count climbs. Root cause lives in the crashed instance's logs + exit code.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA — CrashLoopBackOff means the container RAN and then EXITED. Contrast with ImagePullBackOff (never ran).
Because it keeps dying, try to read the PREVIOUS instance's logs:  kubectl logs <pod> --previous

EXIT CODE CHEATSHEET
  0    clean exit — BUT a Deployment restarts its container even on exit 0. If the process isn't meant
       to be long-running (no server/sleep/blocking call), it'll cycle forever even with zero errors.
  1    generic app error (bad config, missing env var, unhandled exception) — READ THE LOGS
  137  SIGKILL (128+9) -> almost always OOMKilled (hit memory limit) — check describe 'Reason: OOMKilled'
  139  SIGSEGV (128+11) -> segfault / bad binary
  143  SIGTERM (128+15) -> graceful shutdown didn't finish in time

GOTCHAS I HIT DURING PRACTICE
  • 'logs --previous' can fail with 'unable to retrieve container logs' — on a FAST crashloop the
    kubelet garbage-collects the dead container's logs before you get to read them. Fallback: run
    'kubectl logs' WITHOUT --previous to catch the current/latest attempt, and rely on describe's
    Last State + Exit Code as the source of truth if logs are gone entirely. Production takeaway:
    ship logs to Cloud Logging / a log aggregator so crash evidence survives the restart.
  • Deployment 'Reason' field has two places it shows up: 'State: Waiting / Reason: CrashLoopBackOff'
    is the CURRENT wait reason; 'Last State: Terminated / Reason: OOMKilled|Error / Exit Code: N' is
    the ACTUAL cause. Don't confuse the two — the top-level Reason just says 'it's looping', the
    Last State Reason says WHY.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: Pod is CrashLoopBackOff — steps?
A: get pods (RESTARTS climbing) -> describe (Last State: Terminated + Exit Code + Reason) -> logs
   (--previous, fall back to current if GC'd) -> fix the app/config/resource cause.

Q: How do you tell OOMKilled from an app crash?
A: describe shows Reason: OOMKilled and Exit Code: 137, no app log line (kernel kills it, app never
   gets to log). App crash is usually Exit Code: 1 with a clear error line in the logs.

Q: Container exits 0 but the pod keeps restarting — why?
A: restartPolicy on a Deployment's pods is effectively Always — even a clean exit is treated as
   'container needs restarting'. The image/command must be a long-running process (server, daemon,
   sleep loop) or it doesn't belong in a Deployment (use a Job/CronJob instead for run-once work).

Q: Liveness probe causing restarts — how would you spot it?
A: Events show 'Liveness probe failed' + 'Killing container'. Container may be healthy but slow to
   start -> add/raise initialDelaySeconds or use a startupProbe.

Q: OOMKilled — how do you decide whether to raise the limit or fix the app?
A: If real, expected usage genuinely exceeds an arbitrarily-set limit -> raise the limit (with
   headroom, backed by kubectl top / metrics history). If usage is unbounded / a leak -> fix the app;
   raising the limit only delays the same crash.

Q: Exit Code 137 always means OOMKilled?
A: No — 137 = SIGKILL from ANY source. A liveness-probe-triggered kill also reports Exit Code: 137 on
   the terminated container, same as an OOM kill. Don't stop at the exit code — check Events for
   'Unhealthy'/'Killing' (probe kill) vs describe's 'Reason: OOMKilled' (memory kill). Reading only
   the exit code here is the classic misdiagnosis trap.

Q: App logs look completely clean but the pod still keeps restarting — what does that tell you?
A: Clean logs + climbing RESTARTS is itself a signal: the app isn't erroring, something EXTERNAL is
   killing it. Go straight to Events for 'Killing'/'Unhealthy' (liveness probe) or 'OOMKilled'
   (memory) rather than re-reading app logs looking for an error that isn't there.

Q: Liveness probe keeps killing a slow-booting app — what's the RIGHT fix, not just the quick one?
A: Quick patch: raise initialDelaySeconds/failureThreshold on the livenessProbe. Proper fix: add a
   startupProbe with its own generous failureThreshold/periodSeconds for boot time — liveness only
   starts being enforced AFTER the startupProbe first succeeds. This keeps liveness strict/fast for
   detecting real hangs later, without needing a loose initialDelaySeconds that slows down that
   detection too.

problems.title: Starts, then dies — missing env var
problems.symptom: The 'api' deployment was healthy in staging but won't stay up here. The pod keeps restarting — RESTARTS climbs every minute, never Ready. On-call needs root cause before paging the app team.
problems.hint: It DOES start a container, so describe shows Last State: Terminated with an Exit Code. The code says it failed; the WHY is in logs — try --previous first to read the instance that just died.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> STATUS=CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS climbing. describe pod -> Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error, Exit Code: 1. logs --previous -> often 'unable to retrieve container logs' if the dead container was already GC'd (common on fast loops) -> fall back to 'kubectl logs' without --previous -> 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set. api cannot start.'
problems.rootCause: Two stacked issues found in practice: (1) required env var DATABASE_URL isn't provided, so the app deliberately exits 1 on startup when it's absent. (2) a second latent bug — if the container script has no long-running command (e.g. a dropped 'sleep'), fixing #1 alone makes it exit 0 instead, and the Deployment restarts it anyway since exit 0 still counts as 'needs restarting'.
problems.fix: Provide the missing config (kubectl set env for a quick patch; a Secret/ConfigMap via envFrom for the proper declarative fix). Separately, make sure the container command actually blocks / stays alive (sleep, or a real server process) — an exit-0 one-liner does not belong directly in a Deployment.
problems.mental: CrashLoop = ran then exited. Exit code narrows it (1=app/config, 137=OOM). logs --previous is high-value but can be GC'd on fast loops — always have 'describe Last State' as your fallback source of truth. And remember: exit 0 still restarts in a Deployment.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
# api container exits 1 when $DATABASE_URL is empty

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                          # CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS climbing
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=api           # Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error, Exit Code: 1
kubectl logs -n drill -l app=api --previous        # may fail: 'unable to retrieve container logs' (GC'd)
kubectl logs -n drill -l app=api                   # fallback: current attempt -> 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set'

commands.label: Fix (quick patch)
commands.code:
kubectl set env -n drill deployment/api DATABASE_URL='postgres://demo'
# also ensure the container has a blocking command (sleep/server), not just an echo, or exit 0 keeps restarting it
kubectl rollout status -n drill deployment/api
kubectl get pods -n drill                          # 1/1 Running, RESTARTS stops

commands.label: Fix (proper / declarative)
commands.code:
# store config in a Secret, reference it from the Deployment:
kubectl create secret generic api-cfg -n drill --from-literal=DATABASE_URL='postgres://demo'
# then in the container spec:
#   envFrom:
#   - secretRef: { name: api-cfg }

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Crashes exactly when traffic/load picks up — OOMKilled
problems.symptom: The 'cache' deployment in drill keeps restarting. It comes up fine for a few seconds, then dies. No app logs, nothing useful in kubectl logs. Team swears the code hasn't changed — 'it just crashes now.'
problems.hint: describe -> Last State: Terminated -> look at the Reason field right next to Exit Code, not just the code itself. 137 is a very specific number (128 + signal 9).
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS climbing, no error events (just repeated Pulled/Created/Started/BackOff — a sign the kill comes from outside the app). describe -> Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. Limits/Requests show memory: 52Mi while the workload (stress --vm-bytes 200M) deliberately allocates 200MB.
problems.rootCause: The container's memory limit (52Mi) is far below what the workload actually allocates (200MB). The kernel's cgroup memory controller SIGKILLs the process the instant it crosses the limit — before the app gets any chance to log an error, which is why kubectl logs looks empty.
problems.fix: Raise the memory limit (and matching request) to comfortably cover real usage, confirmed via kubectl top. If this were a real leak instead of expected usage, the correct fix would be fixing the app's memory growth, not just raising the ceiling — raising the limit on a genuine leak only delays the same crash.
problems.mental: No app-level error + repeating Created/Started/BackOff events + Exit Code 137 = OOM, every time. Reason: OOMKilled is the confirming field — don't stop at the exit code alone. Decide 'raise limit' vs 'fix app' by whether usage is bounded/expected or unbounded/leaking.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
# container requests+limits memory: 52Mi but stress --vm-bytes 200M allocates 200MB

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=cache | sed -n '/^Containers:/,/^Conditions:/p'   # State/Last State/Reason/Exit Code
kubectl top pod -n drill                  # live memory usage vs limit (needs metrics-server)

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl patch deployment cache -n drill --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"300Mi"},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/memory","value":"300Mi"}
]'
kubectl rollout status -n drill deployment/cache
kubectl get pods -n drill                 # 1/1 Running, RESTARTS stops climbing
kubectl top pod -n drill                  # confirm usage sits under the new limit

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: It's healthy, but Kubernetes keeps killing it — bad liveness probe
problems.symptom: The 'slow-start' service in drill never stabilizes. Restart count keeps climbing. kubectl logs shows totally normal startup output — no errors, no stack trace, nothing. The app team insists their code works fine locally. Ops wants to know why Kubernetes keeps killing a healthy process.
problems.hint: Last State -> Reason won't say Error or OOMKilled in an obviously distinct way here — Exit Code is still 137. Look for the word 'Killing' in Events, not Last State. Check the timing: how long does the app actually take to become ready vs when Kubernetes first checks it?
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> CrashLoopBackOff/climbing RESTARTS, logs are completely clean (a signal the app itself isn't erroring). describe Events show: 'Unhealthy: Liveness probe failed: ... connection refused' followed by 'Killing: Container ... failed liveness probe, will be restarted'. Last State shows Exit Code: 137 (same code as an OOM kill — a trap if you don't check Events).
problems.rootCause: The app has a real ~25s boot sequence (sleep 25 before the HTTP server binds), but the livenessProbe starts checking at initialDelaySeconds: 5 with failureThreshold: 1 — zero tolerance. Every check before the server is actually listening gets 'connection refused' and instantly kills the container, which was never actually unhealthy — it just hadn't finished starting.
problems.fix: Quick patch: raise initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold on the livenessProbe so it stops checking before the app can possibly be ready. Proper production fix: add a startupProbe with its own generous failureThreshold/periodSeconds for boot time; livenessProbe only starts being enforced after the startupProbe first succeeds, so liveness itself can stay strict/fast for genuinely detecting hangs later.
problems.mental: Exit Code 137 does NOT always mean OOMKilled — it's SIGKILL from any source, and a probe-triggered kill reports the same code. Clean app logs + climbing restarts = something external is killing it; go straight to Events ('Unhealthy'/'Killing') instead of re-reading logs for an error that isn't there.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
# app takes sleep 25 to boot; livenessProbe initialDelaySeconds=5, failureThreshold=1

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=slow-start   # look for Unhealthy + Killing in EVENTS, not Last State
kubectl logs -n drill -l app=slow-start            # clean logs -> tell that it's not app-side

commands.label: Fix (quick patch)
Fix (proper / startupProbe)
commands.code:

#   startupProbe:
#     httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
#     failureThreshold: 30
#     periodSeconds: 2        # allows up to 60s to boot
#   livenessProbe:
#     httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
#     periodSeconds: 5
#     failureThreshold: 1     # can stay strict once startupProbe has passed once

commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Never even reaches CrashLoopBackOff — CreateContainerConfigError
problems.symptom: The 'worker' deployment in drill was just applied. It's not CrashLoopBackOff, not ImagePullBackOff — 'kubectl get pods' shows a status you don't see every day. RESTARTS is 0. No logs exist at all.
problems.hint: RESTARTS is 0 because the container has never actually STARTED, not even once — this fails a step earlier than a crash. Whatever it is, it's blocking the container from being created in the first place.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> STATUS: CreateContainerConfigError, RESTARTS: 0 (never ran, so --previous and even current logs are both empty — 'kubectl logs' errors with 'container has not been created'). describe pod -> Events: 'Error: couldn't find key API_TOKEN in Secret drill/worker-secret'.
problems.rootCause: The container's envFrom/env references a specific KEY inside an existing Secret (API_TOKEN), but that key was never actually put in the Secret — the Secret object itself exists, just without that entry. Kubelet validates that every referenced key resolves BEFORE creating the container at all, so this fails earlier and differently than an app-level crash: no image pull happened, no process ever ran, no logs were ever produced.
problems.fix: Add the missing key to the Secret (or fix the key NAME if it was just a typo against what's actually stored), then let kubelet retry — no rollout or image change needed, since the container spec itself was correct; the referenced data just wasn't there yet.
problems.mental: CreateContainerConfigError sits in its own bucket, earlier than CrashLoopBackOff: RESTARTS is 0 forever until the config is fixed, because kubelet refuses to even START the container on a Config/Secret key it can't resolve. Contrast with the earlier missing-env-var drill, where the container DID start and then exited 1 from inside the app — this one never gets that far.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create secret generic worker-secret --from-literal=OTHER_KEY=placeholder   # API_TOKEN deliberately missing
kubectl -n drill create deployment worker --image=busybox --replicas=1 -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n drill patch deployment worker --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env","value":[{"name":"API_TOKEN","valueFrom":{"secretKeyRef":{"name":"worker-secret","key":"API_TOKEN"}}}]}]'

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                        # CreateContainerConfigError, RESTARTS 0
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=worker      # Events: couldn't find key API_TOKEN in Secret
kubectl logs -n drill -l app=worker              # errors — container was never created, nothing to show

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl -n drill patch secret worker-secret --type=merge -p '{"stringData":{"API_TOKEN":"demo-token-123"}}'
kubectl get pods -n drill -w                     # kubelet retries automatically, no rollout needed -> 1/1 Running

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Main container never even starts — failing init container
problems.symptom: The 'gateway' deployment in drill is stuck at READY 0/1. 'kubectl logs' on the obvious container name comes back empty/normal — but the pod has clearly never served traffic. STATUS shows something other than Running or CrashLoopBackOff.
problems.hint: Check what CONTAINERS this pod actually has, not just the one you expect. 'kubectl get pods' has a column for how many init containers have completed out of how many exist.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> STATUS: Init:CrashLoopBackOff (or Init:Error), READY 0/1. describe pod -> Init Containers section shows 'wait-for-db' with Last State: Terminated, Exit Code: 1 — the MAIN container ('gateway') is still Waiting, PodInitializing, and has never started at all. logs on the main container name fails with 'container has not been created'; logs -c wait-for-db -> 'could not connect to db:5432, retrying...'.
problems.rootCause: Init containers run to completion, IN ORDER, before the main container starts at all — the main container will not even be attempted until every init container exits 0. Here, the 'wait-for-db' init container is looping trying to reach a database Service (db) that was never actually created in this namespace, so it never succeeds, and the main gateway container is permanently blocked behind it despite being perfectly correct itself.
problems.fix: Fix what the failing init container is actually waiting on — here, create the missing db Service/dependency it's polling for. The main container needs zero changes; it was never the problem, it just never got a turn.
problems.mental: An init container failure LOOKS like the main container is crashing (READY 0/1, restarts climbing) but the diagnostic path is completely different — go straight to the Init Containers section of describe, not the main container's logs, which will be empty or error out because that container was never created. 'kubectl get pods' READY column combined with a STATUS starting with 'Init:' is the fastest tell.

cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

problems.title: Instantly Error, every single time — bad entrypoint (exit 127)
problems.symptom: The 'notifier' deployment in drill goes straight to CrashLoopBackOff within seconds of being applied — no slow boot, no probe involved, it never even gets a chance to do anything. RESTARTS climbs almost instantly.
problems.hint: This one doesn't need --previous or any deep digging — the exit code itself is unusual and specific. It's not 1, not 137, not 143. Look it up rather than assuming it's a generic app error.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS climbing within seconds each time. describe pod -> Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error, Exit Code: 127. logs -> '/bin/sh: pyhton: not found' (sic).
problems.rootCause: The container's command overrides the image's entrypoint with a typo'd binary name ('pyhton' instead of 'python'). Exit Code 127 is the shell's own convention for 'command not found' — this fails before the application ever gets a chance to run any of its own code, which is why it's instant and identical on every single restart.
problems.fix: Correct the typo in the Deployment's command field and roll out. Because this is a pure spec error (not an environmental/config dependency), the fix is entirely in the manifest — no external resource to create, no secret to patch.
problems.mental: Exit 127 is its own distinct, high-signal code — 'command not found', almost always a typo'd binary name or a missing executable in a slim/distroless image that doesn't have the shell utility you assumed it did. It fails FAST and IDENTICALLY every time (no variance run to run), unlike a flaky/probe-related crash — that instant, consistent failure pattern is itself a diagnostic clue pointing at the command/entrypoint rather than app logic.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create deployment notifier --image=python:3.12-slim --replicas=1 -- pyhton -m http.server 8080

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                             # CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS climbs in seconds
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=notifier         # Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error, Exit Code: 127
kubectl logs -n drill -l app=notifier                 # /bin/sh: pyhton: not found

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl patch deployment notifier -n drill --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/command","value":["python","-m","http.server","8080"]}]'
kubectl rollout status -n drill deployment/notifier
kubectl get pods -n drill                             # 1/1 Running

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

data.name: Service & Networking
data.desc: Pods are healthy — Running, 0 restarts — but traffic still fails. The problem lives between the Service and its endpoints: readiness gating, selectors, load-balancing. Nothing crashes, so logs look clean; the answer is in endpoints + Events, not logs.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA — a pod can be Running, 0 restarts, and STILL be pulled out of traffic. Readiness != Liveness:
  • livenessProbe fails  -> kubelet KILLS & restarts the container (RESTARTS climb, Exit 137)
  • readinessProbe fails -> pod marked NotReady, its IP is REMOVED from the Service endpoints;
    the container is NOT restarted. No crash, no restart — just silent traffic loss.

THE TELL: READY column flaps 1/1 <-> 0/1 while RESTARTS stays 0. Then go read the Service's endpoints.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: Pods are Running with 0 restarts but users get intermittent 502s — where do you look?
A: The Service's endpoints/endpointslices. Flapping readiness silently removes pod IPs from LB rotation.

Q: Difference between liveness and readiness probes?
A:Liveness probe checks whether the application is still alive and functioning. If the liveness probe keeps failing, Kubernetes assumes the container is stuck or unhealthy and restarts the container. Readiness probe checks whether the application is ready to receive traffic. If readiness fails, Kubernetes does not restart the container; instead, Kubernetes removes that Pod from the Service's endpoints, so traffic is not sent to it until it becomes ready again. Easy way to remember: Liveness = “Should I restart you?” Readiness = “Should I send traffic to you?” 

Liveness = 'is it alive?' fail -> restart. Readiness = 'can it serve?' fail -> remove from Service
   endpoints, no restart. startupProbe gates both during boot.

Q: A Service exists and pods are Running, but 'kubectl get endpoints' is empty — why?
A: No READY pods match the selector — either readiness is failing, or the selector/labels don't match.

Q: Why is coupling readiness to a downstream DB check dangerous?
A: A momentary DB latency spike makes readiness fail -> pods drop out of LB -> cascading traffic loss,
   even though the app itself is fine. Keep readiness shallow; cache downstream health.

problems.title: Healthy pods, but users get intermittent 502s — flaky readiness
problems.symptom: The 'checkout' service in drill is up — all pods Running, RESTARTS 0, no CrashLoop. But users hit intermittent 502s / connection resets. Sometimes checkout works, sometimes it doesn't. 'kubectl get pods' looks totally healthy. On-call is stumped because nothing is obviously broken.
problems.hint: Watch the READY column, not RESTARTS — it flickers 1/1 <-> 0/1. The container is never killed, so this is NOT a crash or a liveness kill. Go look at what the Service actually has as backends.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -w -> READY flaps 1/1 <-> 0/1 across all 3 pods, RESTARTS stays 0, no CrashLoop. get endpoints checkout -> address count is short (e.g. 2 of 3) at any given moment, changing second to second. describe pod -> Events show repeated 'Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503' (dozens of times in a few minutes), but NO 'Liveness probe failed', NO 'Killing', RESTARTS 0. The /healthz endpoint has a built-in 40% random chance of returning 503 with failureThreshold=1 and periodSeconds=3s — zero tolerance, checked every 3s.
problems.rootCause: The readiness probe hits an endpoint that's deliberately/effectively flaky (real-world equivalent: a shallow check coupled to something unreliable, e.g. a slow downstream). Because failureThreshold=1, a SINGLE bad check (40% chance, every 3s) is enough to flip a perfectly healthy pod to NotReady -> the endpoint controller yanks its IP out of the Service's endpoints -> fewer backends -> intermittent 5xx for whoever's request lands during that window. The container is never restarted (readiness, not liveness), so RESTARTS/CrashLoop tells stay silent the whole time.
problems.fix: Raise failureThreshold (e.g. 1 -> 3) so a pod needs multiple consecutive bad checks before being pulled — since each check only has a 40% failure chance, 3-in-a-row is far rarer than 1 alone, so healthy pods stop getting falsely evicted while a genuinely broken pod still gets caught. Production fix: make the readiness endpoint a SHALLOW self-check, not coupled to something with its own failure rate — or cache a downstream health result instead of checking it live on every probe.
problems.mental: Contrast with the liveness drill: liveness fail KILLS & restarts (RESTARTS climb, Exit 137); readiness fail NEVER restarts — it silently evicts the pod from load balancing. Same probe family, opposite failure signature. Healthy pods + intermittent 5xx = go straight to endpoints, not logs. CONFIRM LIVE with 'watch -n1 kubectl get endpoints' — watching the address count/list actually change second-to-second is the clearest proof of the mechanism. Unrelated noise to expect: 'FailedScheduling' events (Insufficient memory / untolerated taints) followed by a 'Scheduled' event just means GKE Autopilot's Node Auto-Provisioning was spinning up a new node to fit the pods — not part of this bug, resolves on its own.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl apply -n drill -f checkout.yaml
# /healthz has a 40% random chance of returning 503
# readinessProbe: periodSeconds=3, failureThreshold=1 (zero tolerance)

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill -l app=checkout -w                                  # READY flaps 1/1 <-> 0/1, RESTARTS stays 0
kubectl get endpoints checkout -n drill                                       # address count is short/changing
watch -n1 "kubectl get endpoints checkout -n drill"                           # WATCH IT LIVE — count/addresses change every few seconds
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=checkout -n drill -o yaml   # ready:true/false per address, explicit
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=checkout                                 # Events: repeated 'Readiness probe failed... statuscode: 503' — NO Killing, RESTARTS 0
kubectl logs -n drill <pod-name> -f                                           # (this toy app logs every /healthz hit — watch 200s/503s alternate live)

Fix (proper, production)

# keep liveness (process alive) and readiness (can serve) as SEPARATE endpoints
kubectl create pdb checkout-pdb -n drill --selector=app=checkout --min-available=2

problems.title: Service exists, pods are Running — but endpoints is completely empty
problems.symptom: The 'orders' Service in drill has been up for 20 minutes. Every 'orders' pod shows 1/1 Running. But nothing can reach it — every request times out, like the Service isn't backed by anything at all.
problems.hint: A Service doesn't know about pods by name — it finds them by matching its selector against pod LABELS. Check that the two actually agree, character for character.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -n drill -l app=orders -> pods genuinely 1/1 Running. get endpoints orders -n drill -> ENDPOINTS column is completely empty, <none>. describe svc orders -> Selector: app=orders-api. describe pod -> Labels: app=orders. The selector and the pod label don't match — orders-api vs orders.
problems.rootCause: The Service's selector (app=orders-api) doesn't match any pod's actual labels (app=orders) — a naming drift between the Service manifest and the Deployment's pod template, most often from one being edited without the other. Kubernetes doesn't error on this; a Service with a selector matching zero pods is completely valid and silently produces an empty endpoints list — Running pods and an empty Service coexist without any alarm.
problems.fix: Correct the mismatch on whichever side is wrong — usually easiest to fix the Service's selector to match the pod's real labels, since changing pod labels means a rollout. Confirm afterward with 'kubectl get endpoints' actually listing pod IPs, not just that the Service 'looks' fine.
problems.mental: Empty endpoints with healthy Running pods is ALWAYS a labels-vs-selector problem or a readiness problem — nothing else produces this exact combination. Check the selector match first (it's a single describe + describe away); readiness gating (the earlier drill) is the other candidate if the selector genuinely matches but pods aren't Ready.

commands.label: Setup (break it)

kubectl -n drill create deployment orders --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2

apiVersion: v1

  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 80 }]

kubectl describe svc orders -n drill                # Selector: app=orders-api
kubectl get pods -n drill --show-labels             # actual pod label is app=orders, not orders-api

kubectl get endpoints orders -n drill                # now lists real pod IPs

problems.title: Everything's Running, but nothing can resolve the Service's name
problems.symptom: Pods in the 'drill' namespace can't reach the 'inventory' Service by name — the app logs show connection errors mentioning a hostname that never resolves. Curling the Service's ClusterIP directly works fine.
problems.hint: If the IP works but the NAME doesn't, this isn't a Service or endpoints problem at all — Service DNS is a completely separate mechanism (CoreDNS) from whether the Service itself is correctly wired to pods.
problems.diagnosis: exec into a pod and curl the Service's ClusterIP directly -> works. nslookup inventory from the same pod -> 'server can't find inventory: NXDOMAIN'. nslookup inventory.wrong-ns.svc.cluster.local (a namespace it's NOT in) -> also fails, as expected. get svc inventory -n drill -> exists, ClusterIP assigned normally. Checking the app's client code shows it's calling the Service from a DIFFERENT namespace than the Service actually lives in, using just the short name with no namespace suffix.
problems.rootCause: Kubernetes' short-form Service DNS (just the Service name, no suffix) only resolves within the SAME namespace the querying pod is in — cluster-internal DNS names are actually '<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local', and the short form is a search-domain convenience that only works when both sides share a namespace. A caller in a different namespace using the bare short name will always get NXDOMAIN, even though the exact same Service resolves fine for anything inside its own namespace.
problems.fix: Use the fully-qualified name (inventory.drill.svc.cluster.local) — or at minimum the namespaced short form (inventory.drill) — from callers outside the Service's namespace. Within the same namespace, the bare short name is fine and is what most examples/tutorials show, which is exactly why this trips people up the first time they call cross-namespace.
problems.mental: ClusterIP curl working + DNS name failing isolates the problem to CoreDNS/naming specifically, ruling out selector/endpoints issues entirely (those would break the IP too). The single most common real-world cause of THIS exact split is a cross-namespace call using the short name — always check both the caller's namespace and the target's namespace before assuming CoreDNS itself is broken.

problems.title: Pods are Ready, endpoints look fine — but a NetworkPolicy is silently dropping the traffic
problems.symptom: The 'ledger' pods in drill are Running, Ready, and show up correctly in 'kubectl get endpoints'. But calls from the 'frontend' pods to ledger time out — no refused connection, no DNS error, just silence until the client gives up.
problems.hint: Everything upstream of the network layer looks correct — pods healthy, endpoints populated, DNS resolves fine. A connection that hangs and times out rather than being actively refused is a classic sign of something silently dropping packets rather than rejecting them.
problems.diagnosis: get pods/get endpoints for ledger both look completely healthy. curl from a frontend pod to ledger's ClusterIP -> hangs, eventually times out (not 'connection refused', which would point elsewhere). get networkpolicy -n drill -> a policy named 'ledger-deny-all' exists, selecting app=ledger, with an empty ingress list — the classic 'deny everything into this pod' baseline policy, and nothing explicitly allows traffic from frontend.
problems.rootCause: NetworkPolicies are additive and default-closed the moment ANY policy selects a pod: with zero NetworkPolicies at all, every pod accepts all traffic; the instant one policy selects a pod, everything NOT explicitly allowed for it is denied. Here, 'ledger-deny-all' selects ledger pods with an empty ingress rule set — which means 'allow nothing in' — and no separate policy exists granting frontend an explicit exception, so its traffic is silently dropped at the CNI layer, never even reaching the container.
problems.fix: Add a NetworkPolicy that explicitly allows ingress to ledger FROM frontend (matched by podSelector/namespaceSelector, not IP — pod IPs are not stable). Don't delete the deny-all baseline itself; layering an explicit allow rule alongside it is the intended pattern, not replacing the whole policy.
problems.mental: A request that TIMES OUT (not refused, not DNS failure) with otherwise-healthy pods and endpoints is the single strongest tell for a NetworkPolicy silently dropping packets — it's invisible to 'kubectl get pods/endpoints' entirely, since neither the pod's health nor the Service's wiring is actually broken. Always check 'kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>' explicitly; there's no 'Events' warning that traffic is being blocked.

commands.label: Setup (break it)

kubectl -n drill create deployment ledger --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1
kubectl -n drill expose deployment ledger --port=80
kubectl -n drill create deployment frontend --image=busybox --replicas=1 -- sleep 3600
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: ledger-deny-all
  namespace: drill
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: ledger } }
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
  ingress: []
EOF

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods,endpoints -n drill                                              # everything looks healthy
kubectl exec -n drill deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 ledger            # hangs, then times out
kubectl get networkpolicy -n drill                                               # ledger-deny-all exists

problems.title: Ingress returns 502 — the pods and Service are both completely fine
problems.symptom: Hitting the 'search' app through its Ingress hostname returns 502 Bad Gateway from the load balancer itself — not from the app. 'kubectl get pods' and 'kubectl get svc' both look totally normal.
problems.hint: A 502 from THIS layer means the load balancer successfully reached something and got a bad response — or couldn't reach anything sane at all. Check what the Ingress is actually POINTING at, not the pods or Service on their own.
problems.diagnosis: get pods/get svc for search both healthy, endpoints populated correctly. describe ingress search -> backend rule points at Service 'search-svc', port 8080. get svc search-svc -> the Service's actual port is 80, not 8080 — the Ingress references a port the Service doesn't expose at all.
problems.rootCause: The Ingress rule's backend service port (8080) doesn't match any port actually exposed by the target Service (80). The load balancer can resolve the Service and see it has healthy endpoints, but the specific PORT it was told to send traffic to on that Service simply doesn't exist — resulting in a 502 from the LB layer itself, distinct from a 5xx the app would generate (which would mean the LB->app path is fine and the app itself errored).
problems.fix: Correct the Ingress's backend port to match a port the Service actually exposes (80), or add a matching port to the Service if 8080 was the intended contract. Confirm with a fresh curl through the Ingress hostname, not just kubectl status, since the GLB layer can take a minute to pick up backend changes.
problems.mental: A 502 that originates from the load balancer/Ingress layer (not the app) always means the LB->Service->pod chain is broken somewhere BEFORE the app gets the request — port mismatches (this drill), an Ingress pointing at the wrong Service name entirely, or unhealthy backends per the LB's own health check are the usual suspects. Healthy pods and a healthy Service prove the chain is fine FROM the Service down — the break here is specifically between Ingress and Service.

problems.title: Endpoints are populated, connections still refused — targetPort mismatch
problems.symptom: The 'session-api' Service in drill has real pod IPs listed under endpoints — unlike the earlier empty-endpoints drill, this one genuinely looks wired up. But every connection through the Service gets refused immediately, not a timeout.
problems.hint: Endpoints being populated only proves the selector matched real, Ready pods. It says nothing about whether the PORT the Service forwards to is actually the port the container is listening on inside the pod.
problems.diagnosis: get endpoints session-api -> real pod IPs listed, e.g. 10.4.0.12:9090. Connections refused immediately (not hanging) when curling the Service. exec into the pod, check what it's actually listening on -> the container binds to :8080, not :9090. describe svc -> targetPort: 9090.
problems.rootCause: The Service's targetPort (9090) doesn't match the port the container process actually listens on inside the pod (8080). Endpoints still populate correctly because endpoint generation is driven purely by the selector matching Ready pods — it has no awareness of what port the container is actually bound to internally. The connection reaching the pod's IP on 9090 gets an immediate refusal from the OS, since nothing is listening there — a fundamentally different signature from a NetworkPolicy silently dropping packets (that hangs; this refuses instantly).
problems.fix: Set targetPort to match what the container genuinely listens on (8080). No pod/Deployment change needed at all — this is entirely a Service-side field, and the fix takes effect immediately without a rollout.
problems.mental: Populated endpoints only prove the LABEL match worked — never assume it also proves the PORT is right. Immediate 'connection refused' (vs a NetworkPolicy's silent timeout) is the tell that something IS listening at that IP but not on that specific port. Always cross-check targetPort against what the container's own process actually binds to, not what the manifest author assumed.

data.name: Pending & Unschedulable Pods
data.desc: The pod never even starts — READY 0/1, STATUS Pending, no container ever runs, so there are no logs at all. The answer lives in the pod's Conditions/Events and in what the cluster-autoscaler decided, not in anything the app did.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA — Pending does NOT automatically mean 'wait for autoscaling.' Two Pending pods can look identical
in 'kubectl get pods' and mean completely opposite things:
  • genuinely transient -> autoscaler is actively provisioning a node -> resolves in a minute or two
  • permanently stuck    -> the constraint can NEVER be satisfied by any node -> waiting fixes nothing

THE TELL: read the Events, specifically who says what:
  scheduler event  'FailedScheduling: 0/N nodes are available...'      -> no CURRENT node matches
  autoscaler event 'TriggeredScaleUp'                                  -> actively trying to fix it, wait
  autoscaler event 'NotTriggerScaleUp'                                 -> it looked and REFUSED to try
  annotation 'cloud.google.com/cluster_autoscaler_unhelpable_until: Inf' -> permanent verdict, in writing

GKE AUTOPILOT GUARDRAILS — most 'break the schedule' mistakes get REJECTED before they ever become a
pod, instead of silently sitting Pending like on Standard GKE. Three real ones hit during practice:
  1. Arbitrary/custom nodeSelector key (e.g. 'disktype') -> rejected at admission by GKE Warden.
     Autopilot only allows a specific label-key allowlist (cloud.google.com/compute-class,
     cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator, topology.kubernetes.io/zone, etc. — see error for full list).
  2. Resource request above the per-pod ceiling (this cluster: 30 CPU / 110Gi memory) -> rejected at
     admission, 'higher than the Autopilot maximum'. Never even reaches Pending.
  3. A GPU nodeSelector (cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator) WITHOUT an actual GPU resource request on
     the container -> rejected: 'not allowed on workloads that do not request GPU'.
  -> To actually reproduce a genuine, permanent Pending on Autopilot, use an ALLOWED key with an
     IMPOSSIBLE value instead, e.g. topology.kubernetes.io/zone set to a zone that doesn't exist.
     Warden only validates the KEY is on its allowlist, not that the VALUE corresponds to anything real.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: A pod's Pending and someone says 'just wait, autoscaler will handle it' — how do you know if that's true?
A: Don't guess — read the autoscaler's own event. TriggeredScaleUp means trust it. NotTriggerScaleUp
   (or an 'unhelpable_until: Inf' annotation) means it already gave up; only a spec fix will help.

Q: Why does GKE Autopilot reject some bad specs immediately instead of leaving them Pending?
A: Autopilot runs an admission webhook (GKE Warden) that validates certain fields — like node-selector
   keys and per-pod resource ceilings — at request time, before the object is even persisted. Standard
   GKE has no such gate, so the same mistake there would just sit Pending with FailedScheduling events
   instead of being rejected outright.

Q: What's the fastest way to prove a Pending pod can never schedule, without waiting it out?
A: 'kubectl describe pod' — check Conditions for 'PodScheduled: False', check Events for repeated
   identical FailedScheduling reasons with NO progress between them, and check for the
   cluster_autoscaler_unhelpable_until annotation. Repetition with zero change = stuck, not slow.

problems.title: Pending forever — a zone that doesn't exist
problems.symptom: The 'stuck-pod' deployment in drill was applied over 20 minutes ago. READY is 0/1, STATUS Pending. Someone in the team channel says 'relax, Autopilot's probably just spinning up a node for it, give it a few more minutes.' Do you wait, or is something actually wrong?
problems.hint: Don't just wait it out. There's a real difference between 'the autoscaler is actively working on this' and 'this pod can never be scheduled, no matter how long you wait' — and the Events tell you which one you're looking at.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -n drill -> stuck-pod is 0/1 Pending, climbing in age with no change. describe pod -> Conditions show 'PodScheduled: False'. Events show repeated 'FailedScheduling: 0/N nodes are available: N node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector' — same reason, over and over, no progress. Critically, the autoscaler's own events say 'NotTriggerScaleUp' (not 'TriggeredScaleUp'), and the pod carries the annotation 'cloud.google.com/cluster_autoscaler_unhelpable_until: Inf'. Node-Selectors shows 'topology.kubernetes.io/zone=asia-south1-z' — but the cluster's real zones are only -a, -b, -c.
problems.rootCause: The deployment's nodeSelector requests a zone (asia-south1-z) that does not exist anywhere on GCP — a fabricated value, not a real capacity constraint. The scheduler correctly finds zero matching nodes every time it checks, and the cluster-autoscaler correctly concludes it can never create a matching node either (since no such zone exists to create one in), so it explicitly marks the pod unhelpable rather than repeatedly retrying. This is fundamentally different from a real NAP delay, where the autoscaler IS actively provisioning and the pod resolves within a minute or two.
problems.fix: Remove (or correct) the impossible nodeSelector so the pod template no longer references a nonexistent zone. Once removed, the Deployment controller rolls a new/matching ReplicaSet whose pods have no impossible constraint and schedule normally onto existing nodes.
problems.mental: Same starting symptom (Pending) can mean two opposite things — the deciding signal is the autoscaler's own verdict, not how long you've waited. TriggeredScaleUp = actively fixing itself, let it run. NotTriggerScaleUp + 'unhelpable_until: Inf' = already gave up, permanently — only a spec change fixes it. Bonus finding: GKE Autopilot's Warden webhook actively rejects several classes of impossible spec (arbitrary nodeSelector keys, over-ceiling resource requests, GPU selector without GPU request) at admission time rather than letting them sit Pending — so on Autopilot specifically, if something rejects outright with a clear error, that's Warden doing you a favor, not a bug.

# an impossible (but admission-allowed) constraint: a zone that doesn't exist in this region

problems.title: Pending forever — nothing in the cluster is big enough
problems.symptom: The 'analytics' deployment in drill is stuck Pending. Unlike the earlier drill, there's no weird nodeSelector anywhere in the manifest — it's a completely plain spec. Why won't it schedule?
problems.hint: A plain spec can still be unschedulable if the resource REQUESTS it's asking for are simply bigger than anything the cluster can ever provide, on any node — check what the pod is actually requesting against real node capacity, not just whether the manifest looks normal.
problems.diagnosis: describe pod -> Events: 'FailedScheduling: 0/N nodes are available: N Insufficient cpu, N Insufficient memory'. get nodes -o wide + describe node on the largest one -> Allocatable cpu/memory both well below what the pod requests (e.g. pod requests 16 CPU, largest node allocatable is ~8 CPU). Autoscaler event (on Autopilot/NAP) shows an attempt to provision, but even a freshly provisioned node tops out below the request.
problems.rootCause: The container's resources.requests (16 CPU) exceeds the maximum CPU any single node in this cluster/region's available machine types can ever provide as Allocatable capacity. This is a genuine capacity ceiling, not a config mistake the scheduler can work around — a Pod can never span multiple nodes, so no amount of waiting or additional nodes fixes a request that's bigger than the biggest possible single node.
problems.fix: Lower the resource request to something realistic for the actual workload (confirmed via kubectl top on a similar running instance, not guessed), or — if that request is genuinely necessary — use a machine family/size explicitly big enough, which on Autopilot means requesting a compute class that supports larger allocatable capacity rather than hoping node auto-provisioning finds something that doesn't exist.
problems.mental: Distinguish this from the fake-zone drill by the Events text itself: 'Insufficient cpu/memory' is a genuine capacity ceiling (verify against real node Allocatable, via 'kubectl describe node'), while 'node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector' is a label/selector problem with zero relationship to actual hardware limits. Same Pending status, same FailedScheduling wording style, completely different fix — one needs a smaller/right-sized request, the other needs a corrected selector.

problems.title: Pending on an otherwise-empty node — taint with no matching toleration
problems.symptom: The 'batch' pod in drill is Pending. 'kubectl get nodes' shows plenty of Ready nodes with room to spare — this isn't a capacity problem like the last drill. Something is actively refusing to let this pod land anywhere.
problems.hint: Nodes can carry taints that repel pods unless the pod explicitly says it tolerates that exact taint. Check the nodes for taints, not just their capacity — a taint doesn't show up in 'kubectl top' or Allocatable at all.
problems.diagnosis: describe pod -> Events: 'FailedScheduling: 0/N nodes are available: N node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu: NoSchedule}'. get nodes -o json | grep -A3 taints (or describe on a specific node) -> confirms a node carries taint dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule. The pod spec has no tolerations block at all.
problems.rootCause: A taint on the node (dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule, applied here to reserve a pool for GPU workloads) actively repels any pod that doesn't explicitly tolerate it. The batch pod has zero tolerations, so the scheduler correctly refuses to place it there — and if EVERY node the pod could otherwise fit on carries this same taint, the pod is permanently Pending no matter how much free capacity those nodes have.
problems.fix: Either add a matching toleration to the pod spec (if it genuinely belongs on that reserved pool) or — far more common — this is actually a signal the pod should schedule on a DIFFERENT, untainted node pool instead; the fix is often 'this pod doesn't need the GPU pool at all,' not 'force it past the taint.'
problems.mental: Taints and nodeSelectors solve opposite-shaped problems and produce near-identical Events wording ('node(s) didn't match'/'had untolerated taint') — always read which EXACT phrase appears. A taint problem means the NODE is actively repelling; a selector/affinity problem means the POD is asking for something no node offers. The fix direction is different: tolerations go on the pod to accept a taint; a nodeSelector/affinity value has to actually match something real.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
# taint every node in this small cluster to simulate a fully GPU-reserved pool
for n in $(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do kubectl taint nodes $n dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule --overwrite; done
kubectl -n drill run batch --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600

commands.label: Diagnose
Fix
commands.code:
kubectl -n drill patch pod batch --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/tolerations","value":[{"key":"dedicated","operator":"Equal","value":"gpu","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}]' 2>/dev/null || \
kubectl -n drill run batch2 --image=busybox --restart=Never --overrides='{"spec":{"tolerations":[{"key":"dedicated","operator":"Equal","value":"gpu","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}}' -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pods -n drill                                    # 1/1 Running

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code:
for n in $(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do kubectl taint nodes $n dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule-; done
kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Node drain hangs indefinitely — a PodDisruptionBudget won't let go
problems.symptom: An on-call engineer tries to drain a node in drill ahead of maintenance. 'kubectl drain' just hangs — it never completes, no error, no progress. The node still has pods on it many minutes later.
problems.hint: Draining a node doesn't force-delete pods outright — it EVICTS them, a request that a PodDisruptionBudget is allowed to refuse if honoring it would violate the budget. Check whether something is standing in the way of the eviction itself, not the node.
problems.diagnosis: kubectl drain (in a separate terminal) sits waiting. describe pdb -n drill -> 'checkout-pdb' with minAvailable: 2, currently ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 0 — every one of the 2 checkout replicas is on the SAME node being drained, so evicting any of them would drop available replicas below the budget's minimum, and the eviction API call is being explicitly rejected (429 Too Many Requests) every retry.
problems.rootCause: The 'checkout' Deployment has only 2 replicas, both happen to be scheduled on the single node being drained, and its PodDisruptionBudget requires minAvailable: 2 at all times. Evicting even one pod would violate that guarantee, so the PDB correctly and repeatedly refuses the eviction request — this is the PDB doing exactly its job (protecting availability), not a bug, but it means the drain can never succeed as-is, no matter how long you wait.
problems.fix: Scale the Deployment up temporarily (so losing one replica during drain doesn't violate minAvailable), or spread the existing replicas across multiple nodes to begin with (podAntiAffinity) so a single node drain never holds 100% of a budget-protected workload. Only override the PDB (kubectl drain --disable-eviction, which force-deletes rather than evicts) as a deliberate last resort — it bypasses the exact protection the PDB exists to provide.
problems.mental: A hung drain with no error is the signature of a PDB blocking eviction — very different from a Pending pod (this is about REMOVING a pod, not scheduling one). Always check 'kubectl get pdb -A' and each PDB's ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS count before draining a node in anything but a toy cluster; a PDB silently sitting at 0 allowed disruptions is invisible until you actually try to drain.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create deployment checkout --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl -n drill create pdb checkout-pdb --selector=app=checkout --min-available=2
# for the drill, force both replicas onto the SAME node via a nodeSelector so a single drain affects both
NODE=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl -n drill patch deployment checkout --type=json -p="[{\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector\",\"value\":{\"kubernetes.io/hostname\":\"$NODE\"}}]"

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pdb checkout-pdb -n drill                        # ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 0
kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=30s   # times out / hangs, PDB blocks eviction
kubectl get events -n drill --field-selector reason=FailedEviction --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl -n drill scale deployment checkout --replicas=3     # extra headroom so one eviction no longer violates min-available=2
kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=60s   # succeeds now
kubectl uncordon $NODE

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Pending — asking for a spread the cluster physically can't provide
problems.symptom: The 'inventory-sync' deployment in drill (6 replicas) is stuck with several pods Pending, even though the cluster clearly has free capacity — other pods schedule onto it with no issue at all.
problems.hint: This one isn't about capacity OR taints OR a nonexistent value — it's about a SHAPE constraint. Check whether the deployment is asking the scheduler to distribute pods more evenly across zones/nodes than the cluster's real topology can support.
problems.diagnosis: describe pod (on a Pending one) -> Events: 'FailedScheduling: 0/N nodes are available: N node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints'. get pod -o yaml -> topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule, across a deployment with 6 replicas. get nodes with zone labels -> the cluster only actually spans 2 zones, not the 3+ the constraint's maxSkew:1 effectively requires for 6 replicas to balance evenly.
problems.rootCause: topologySpreadConstraints with whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule is a HARD requirement — maxSkew: 1 across zones means no zone can hold more than 1 extra pod versus the least-loaded zone. With only 2 real zones available but a spread shape that assumes enough zones to keep skew that tight at 6 replicas, the scheduler runs out of zones that would keep skew within the allowed maxSkew and refuses to place the remaining pods at all, rather than violating the constraint.
problems.fix: Either raise maxSkew to something the real zone count can satisfy, or change whenUnsatisfiable to ScheduleAnyway so the constraint becomes a soft preference instead of a hard rule (pods still schedule, just less evenly spread when the ideal shape isn't achievable) — the right choice depends on whether even spread is a genuine hard requirement (e.g. for zone-failure resilience) or just a nice-to-have.
problems.mental: topology spread failures are a fourth distinct Pending root cause alongside insufficient resources, taints, and impossible selector values — the common thread across all four is that 'kubectl describe pod' Events always name the SPECIFIC constraint type in its own words ('Insufficient cpu', 'untolerated taint', 'didn't match node affinity/selector', 'didn't match pod topology spread constraints'). Read that phrase precisely; it tells you which of the four buckets — and which fix — you're in, without any guessing.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: inventory-sync, namespace: drill }
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: inventory-sync } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: inventory-sync } }
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: inventory-sync } }
      containers:
      - name: inventory-sync
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF

kubectl get pods -n drill -o wide                            # some Running, some Pending
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=inventory-sync | grep -A3 FailedScheduling   # didn't match pod topology spread constraints

kubectl rollout status deployment/inventory-sync -n drill

data.name: ConfigMap & Secret Live-Update Gotchas
data.desc: You update a ConfigMap and the running pod keeps behaving like nothing changed — no crash, no error, nothing in the logs. The pod isn't broken; it just never found out. Whether it ever does depends entirely on HOW the ConfigMap was plugged into the container.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA, IN PLAIN ENGLISH — a ConfigMap is a notice board. How a pod reads it decides whether it ever
sees updates to that board after it's already in the room:
  • envFrom / env (environment variable)  -> like handing someone a STICKY NOTE the moment they walk in.
    Whatever's written on it at that second is what they carry for the whole meeting. Nobody comes back
    to hand them a new one just because the board outside changed. NEVER updates. Only a restart
    ('kubectl rollout restart') hands the container a fresh sticky note.
  • volume mount (whole ConfigMap as a directory)  -> like being able to WALK OVER AND READ THE BOARD
    ITSELF whenever you want. kubelet keeps the mounted files in sync with the ConfigMap, roughly once
    a minute. Updates LIVE, no restart needed — but not instantly, there's a real sync delay.
  • volume mount with subPath  -> looks identical to the above, but subPath copies the file's CONTENT
    in at mount time and never re-links it to the live ConfigMap afterward. Same 'looks like it should
    update live' trap as env vars, just less obvious, because it IS a volume mount. NEVER updates.

CONFIRMED IN PRACTICE (drill):
  envFrom            -> exec'd into the pod right after patching the ConfigMap: still the OLD value,
                         forever, until 'kubectl rollout restart'.
  volume mount        -> checked immediately after patching: still old. Checked again ~75s later,
                         no restart in between: NEW value. Confirms the ~1 minute kubelet sync delay.
  volume mount+subPath -> same ConfigMap, same wait, checked again after 75s+: still OLD. subPath
                         silently breaks the live-update mechanism that a plain mount gets for free.

Secrets behave exactly the same way as ConfigMaps here — envFrom/env from a Secret is just as frozen
at container start as it is for a ConfigMap; only volume-mounted Secrets (without subPath) update live.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: You updated a ConfigMap and the app still shows the old value — what's your first question?
A: How is the pod consuming it — env var or volume mount? That single fact decides everything else.
   Env var: it will NEVER update without a restart, full stop. Volume mount: give it up to ~60-90s
   before assuming something's actually wrong.

Q: A ConfigMap is volume-mounted, you've waited two minutes, and it STILL hasn't updated — now what?
A: Check the mount for subPath. It's the single most common reason a volume mount that 'should' be
   live isn't — subPath quietly disables the live-update mechanism.

Q: Why would anyone use subPath if it breaks live updates?
A: subPath is for mounting a SINGLE file into a directory that already has other files in it, without
   the ConfigMap volume overwriting the rest of that directory. It's a legitimate, common need — the
   live-update loss is a side effect most people don't realize they're signing up for.

Q: Does the same logic apply to Secrets?
A: Yes, identically. envFrom/env from a Secret is a one-time snapshot just like a ConfigMap; only a
   plain volume mount (no subPath) gets live updates.

problems.title: ConfigMap says 'on', app still thinks it's 'off'
problems.symptom: The 'config-app' deployment in drill reads a FEATURE_FLAG value from a ConfigMap. On-call updated the ConfigMap ten minutes ago to flip the flag on — 'kubectl get configmap' confirms the new value is definitely saved. But the app is still behaving like the flag is off. No crashes, no restarts, no errors anywhere. What's going on?
problems.hint: The ConfigMap definitely has the new value. So the real question is: where does the running container actually get ITS copy of that value from, and when does it read it — once, or continuously?
problems.diagnosis: get configmap app-config -o yaml -> FEATURE_FLAG really is 'on'. exec into the pod and check its actual environment ('env | grep FEATURE_FLAG') -> still shows 'off'. Comparing the pod's start time against when the ConfigMap was patched shows the pod started BEFORE the update — it was handed its environment at boot and nothing since then has told it to re-read anything.
problems.rootCause: In plain terms: an environment variable sourced from a ConfigMap (via envFrom or env/valueFrom) is like a sticky note handed to the container the instant it starts — whatever the ConfigMap said AT THAT MOMENT is what gets baked in, permanently, for that container's lifetime. Updating the ConfigMap afterward changes the noticeboard, not the sticky note already in the container's hand, and nothing in Kubernetes automatically walks over and swaps it out. This is true even though 'kubectl get configmap' correctly shows the new value — the ConfigMap object itself is fine; the already-running container just never looks at it again after boot.
problems.fix: Force a new container start so it re-reads the (now-updated) ConfigMap fresh: 'kubectl rollout restart deployment/config-app'. For a real production fix, prefer volume-mounting the ConfigMap instead of using env vars wherever the app can tolerate reading a file — that gets you live updates (roughly a 1-minute kubelet sync delay) with zero restarts, as long as the mount does NOT use subPath, which silently disables that same live-update behavior and puts you right back in 'frozen forever' territory.
problems.mental: Three ways to consume the same ConfigMap, three different outcomes — memorize this table: envFrom/env = frozen at container start, restart required, ever; plain volume mount = live updates, ~1 minute lag, no restart needed; volume mount + subPath = looks like a live mount but is actually frozen too, same trap as env vars in disguise. Secrets follow the identical rule — this isn't ConfigMap-specific, it's about env-vars-vs-volumes in general. The single fastest diagnostic question for 'config update isn't taking effect': how is it being consumed, not whether the ConfigMap itself is correct.

commands.label: Setup (break it) — env var version
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create configmap app-config --from-literal=FEATURE_FLAG=off
kubectl -n drill create deployment config-app --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1
kubectl -n drill patch deployment config-app --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/envFrom","value":[{"configMapRef":{"name":"app-config"}}]}]'
kubectl rollout status deployment/config-app -n drill
# simulate the "on-call update, ten minutes later":
kubectl -n drill patch configmap app-config --type=merge -p '{"data":{"FEATURE_FLAG":"on"}}'

commands.label: Diagnose — env var version
commands.code:
kubectl get configmap app-config -n drill -o yaml                 # confirms FEATURE_FLAG: "on" in the ConfigMap itself
kubectl exec -n drill deploy/config-app -- env | grep FEATURE_FLAG # still shows FEATURE_FLAG=off — the mismatch

commands.label: Fix — env var version
commands.code:
kubectl rollout restart deployment/config-app -n drill
kubectl rollout status deployment/config-app -n drill
kubectl exec -n drill deploy/config-app -- env | grep FEATURE_FLAG # now shows FEATURE_FLAG=on

commands.label: Bonus test — plain volume mount (updates live, no restart)
commands.code:
kubectl -n drill patch configmap app-config --type=merge -p '{"data":{"FEATURE_FLAG":"off"}}'
kubectl -n drill patch deployment config-app --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/envFrom","value":[]},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/volumeMounts","value":[{"name":"config-vol","mountPath":"/etc/config"}]},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/volumes","value":[{"name":"config-vol","configMap":{"name":"app-config"}}]}
]'
kubectl rollout status deployment/config-app -n drill
kubectl exec -n drill deploy/config-app -- cat /etc/config/FEATURE_FLAG   # off
kubectl -n drill patch configmap app-config --type=merge -p '{"data":{"FEATURE_FLAG":"on"}}'
