problems.title: Volume-mounted config that STILL never updates — subPath, on its own
problems.symptom: The 'gateway' pod in drill mounts an nginx config file from a ConfigMap — the team specifically chose a volume mount, not env vars, exactly to get live updates without restarting. On-call updates the ConfigMap to fix a bad upstream value. Twenty minutes pass. The pod is still serving the OLD config.
problems.hint: A volume mount SHOULD update live within about a minute — that part of the team's reasoning was correct. So if it's been twenty minutes with zero change, something specific about HOW this particular file is mounted is blocking that normally-automatic behavior.
problems.diagnosis: get configmap nginx-conf -o yaml -> confirms the new value is genuinely saved. exec into the pod, cat the mounted file -> still shows the OLD value, long past the ~60-90s kubelet sync window a plain mount would need. describe pod -> volumeMounts shows subPath: nginx.conf on this specific mount, unlike a directory-style mount.
problems.rootCause: subPath mounts copy the ConfigMap key's CONTENT into the container's filesystem at mount time, as a one-time copy — not a live symlink back to the ConfigMap the way a whole-directory volume mount is. kubelet's periodic sync mechanism that makes plain volume mounts update live specifically does NOT extend to subPath-mounted files, so this file is frozen exactly like an environment variable would be, despite genuinely being a volume mount.
problems.fix: If the app can tolerate it, drop subPath and mount the ConfigMap as a whole directory instead, so kubelet's live-sync applies normally. If subPath is required (e.g. injecting one file into a directory that already has other unrelated files that must not be overwritten), there's no live-update workaround — trigger a 'kubectl rollout restart' after any ConfigMap change instead, the same as you would for an env-var-based config.
problems.mental: This is the same underlying gotcha as the env-var drill, just wearing a volume-mount disguise — 'it's a volume mount' is not sufficient proof that a config will update live; 'it's a volume mount WITHOUT subPath' is the actual condition. Always check for subPath specifically before promising live-update behavior to a team.

problems.title: Not a stale value — the Secret was never there at all
problems.symptom: The 'auth-svc' deployment in drill has never come up, not once — this isn't a case of it working then going stale. It's been stuck since the moment it was applied.
problems.hint: This looks similar to a ConfigMap live-update problem at a glance, but the timeline is different — nothing was ever working. Check whether the thing being referenced actually exists at all, not just whether its value is current.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> CreateContainerConfigError, RESTARTS 0, never ran. describe pod -> Events: 'Error: secret "auth-secrets" not found'. get secret auth-secrets -n drill -> Error from server (NotFound). get secrets -n drill -> a secret named 'auth-secret' (singular) exists — a naming mismatch, not a missing key inside an existing object.
problems.rootCause: The Deployment's envFrom references a Secret object named 'auth-secrets' (plural) that was never created — the actual Secret that WAS created is named 'auth-secret' (singular), a one-character naming drift between the manifest and the actual object. This is a different failure from the earlier missing-KEY drill: there, the Secret object existed and one entry inside it was missing; here, the entire referenced object doesn't exist under that name at all.
problems.fix: Either rename the reference to match the real Secret name, or create a new Secret under the exact name the Deployment expects — whichever is the actual source of truth. Confirm with 'kubectl get secrets' that the name now matches character-for-character; a trailing 's' is easy to miss on a quick read.
problems.mental: CreateContainerConfigError has (at least) two distinct sub-causes that read almost identically in Events: 'key X not found in Secret Y' (Secret exists, one entry inside is missing) versus 'secret Y not found' (the whole object doesn't exist under that name). Both block container creation identically and produce RESTARTS: 0 forever — the exact wording is what tells you whether to check inside an existing Secret or check for a naming typo on the reference itself.

kubectl -n drill create deployment auth-svc --image=busybox --replicas=1 -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n drill patch deployment auth-svc --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/envFrom","value":[{"secretRef":{"name":"auth-secrets"}}]}]'   # referenced as auth-secrets (plural)

kubectl get pods -n drill -w                           # 1/1 Running, no rollout needed beyond the patch itself

commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

data.name: RBAC & Workload Identity
data.desc: A pod is 'set up' to authenticate to Google Cloud — the annotations are there, everything looks connected — but every real API call fails with a permission error. Two separate systems (Kubernetes and Google IAM) both have to agree, and it's easy to configure only one of them.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA, IN PLAIN WORDS — Workload Identity connects a Kubernetes ServiceAccount (KSA) to a real Google
Cloud service account (GSA) so pods can call GCP APIs without a downloaded key file. Setting it up is
TWO separate steps, in TWO separate systems, and doing only one of them LOOKS finished but isn't:
  1. kubectl annotate serviceaccount KSA iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=GSA_EMAIL
     -> tells KUBERNETES which GSA this KSA should claim to be. Purely a Kubernetes-side note.
  2. gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding GSA_EMAIL --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser
     --member "serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA]"
     -> tells GOOGLE IAM that this specific KSA identity is ALLOWED to actually use that GSA. This is
     the approval step, and it lives entirely outside Kubernetes — kubectl can't see or set it.
Skip step 2 and step 1 alone gives you a pod that CLAIMS an identity nothing has approved it to use.

THE TELL, CONFIRMED IN PRACTICE (drill):
  'gcloud auth list' inside the pod -> showed the RIGHT identity (drill-gsa@...) — the annotation (step 1)
  was working fine. The claim was correct; nothing was wrong with it.
  'gcloud projects get-iam-policy ...' -> crashed with a DIFFERENT, unrelated error: 'MetadataServerException
  ... metadata server is concealed'. This is a real, separate gcloud-CLI-on-GKE quirk (metadata
  concealment) — the full gcloud CLI makes extra internal metadata calls that GKE blocks for security,
  independent of any IAM issue. It affects the gcloud CLI specifically, not apps using client libraries.
  Bypassing gcloud and hitting the metadata server directly (the way a real app/library would) —
  'curl -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google" http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/
  service-accounts/default/token' — got straight past that noise, to the REAL error underneath:
  'Unable to generate access token; IAM returned 403 Forbidden: Permission
  iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken denied ... This error could be caused by a missing IAM policy
  binding on the target IAM service account.' — Google's own error message names the exact cause.
  After adding the missing 'roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser' binding, the identical token request
  succeeded — a real JSON blob with an access_token came back, no restart or redeploy needed.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: A pod's ServiceAccount is annotated for Workload Identity but GCP API calls still fail — where do
   you look first?
A: Whether the IAM-side binding exists — 'roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser' granted to
   'PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA]' on the target GSA. The annotation alone only configures the
   Kubernetes side of the handshake; IAM has to separately approve it.

Q: Inside a GKE pod, 'gcloud' commands fail with a metadata-server-concealed error even though
   Workload Identity is set up correctly — is that an auth bug?
A: No — that's a known gcloud-CLI-specific issue on GKE (metadata concealment blocks some of the extra
   metadata queries the full CLI makes). It's unrelated to whether the IAM binding is correct. Test the
   underlying credential directly against the metadata server (or with a client library) instead of
   trusting the gcloud CLI's behavior inside a pod.

Q: What's the practical difference between 'authentication failure' and 'authorization failure' here?
A: A missing workloadIdentityUser binding is an AUTHENTICATION failure — the pod can't even obtain a
   valid token for the GSA at all (403 on getAccessToken itself). A GSA that has a valid token but
   lacks a specific IAM role (e.g. storage.objectViewer) on a resource is an AUTHORIZATION failure —
   the token works, the identity is real, but that identity still isn't allowed to do the specific
   thing being attempted. Same 403-shaped symptom, different layer, different fix.

problems.title: Annotated for Workload Identity, still gets 403 everywhere
problems.symptom: The 'wi-test' pod in drill is set up to authenticate to Google Cloud using Workload Identity — its ServiceAccount (drill-ksa) is annotated to impersonate a real GCP service account (drill-gsa). But every gcloud command run inside the pod fails with a permission/auth error. The annotation is definitely there — 'kubectl describe sa' confirms it. What's missing?
problems.hint: Being ANNOTATED to impersonate a GSA and being ALLOWED to impersonate that GSA are two separate steps in two separate systems. One (Kubernetes) says what identity to claim. The other (Google IAM) says whether that claim is actually approved. Also: if the full gcloud CLI itself crashes with a 'metadata server concealed' error, that's a distraction, not the real answer — go around it and talk to the metadata server directly.
problems.diagnosis: 'gcloud auth list' inside the pod correctly shows drill-gsa@... as the active account — the Kubernetes-side annotation is fine. 'gcloud projects get-iam-policy' crashes with an unrelated MetadataServerException (gcloud-CLI-on-GKE metadata concealment, not an IAM problem). Bypassing gcloud with a direct metadata-server curl for a token instead ('.../service-accounts/default/token') surfaces the real signal: 'Unable to generate access token; IAM returned 403 Forbidden: Permission iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken denied ... This error could be caused by a missing IAM policy binding on the target IAM service account.'
problems.rootCause: Workload Identity setup has two independent halves. The Kubernetes-side annotation (iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=...) was done correctly — it tells the KSA which GSA to claim. But the Google IAM-side approval (granting roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser to the specific KSA identity string, on the GSA) was never done — so IAM has no record of authorizing this KSA to actually obtain credentials for that GSA. Annotating a claim and being permitted to make that claim are enforced by two completely different systems, and doing only the first one produces a pod that LOOKS fully configured while being unable to authenticate at all.
problems.fix: Grant the missing IAM binding: 'gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding GSA_EMAIL --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member "serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA_NAME]"'. No redeploy or pod restart required — re-requesting a token from the metadata server immediately succeeds once the binding exists, since the pod was never misconfigured, IAM was just never told to allow it.
problems.mental: Workload Identity failures split into two distinct layers, and the fix depends on which one you're in: (1) can't get a token at all (this drill) = authentication failure = missing workloadIdentityUser binding, almost always. (2) gets a token fine but a specific API call still 403s = authorization failure = the GSA itself lacks the actual IAM role for that resource — a completely different, later fix. Also remember: the gcloud CLI misbehaving inside a GKE pod (metadata concealment) is a known red herring — test the metadata server directly before concluding anything about IAM.

commands.label: Setup (break it) — annotate but don't grant the IAM binding
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl create serviceaccount drill-ksa -n drill

# create a real GCP service account for this drill
gcloud iam service-accounts create drill-gsa --display-name="Drill Workload Identity test SA" --project=terraform-gke-learning

# link KSA -> GSA on the Kubernetes side (this part IS done correctly)
kubectl annotate serviceaccount drill-ksa -n drill iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=drill-gsa@terraform-gke-learning.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# INTENTIONALLY MISSING: the IAM-side binding that actually allows drill-ksa to impersonate drill-gsa

# deploy a pod using this KSA, with gcloud + curl available inside it
kubectl -n drill run wi-test --image=google/cloud-sdk:slim --restart=Never --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"drill-ksa"}}' -- sleep 3600
kubectl wait -n drill --for=condition=Ready pod/wi-test --timeout=90s

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl exec -n drill wi-test -- gcloud auth list                          # correct identity shown — annotation is fine
kubectl exec -n drill wi-test -- gcloud projects get-iam-policy terraform-gke-learning
  # crashes: MetadataServerException — a gcloud-CLI-on-GKE quirk, NOT the real answer, ignore it

# bypass gcloud entirely, talk to the metadata server directly like a real app/library would:
kubectl exec -n drill wi-test -- sh -c 'curl -s -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google" "http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/email"'
kubectl exec -n drill wi-test -- sh -c 'curl -s -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google" "http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token"'
  # 403: 'Unable to generate access token ... missing IAM policy binding on the target IAM service account'

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding drill-gsa@terraform-gke-learning.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member "serviceAccount:terraform-gke-learning.svc.id.goog[drill/drill-ksa]" \
  --project=terraform-gke-learning

# no restart needed — re-request the token, same pod, same command:
kubectl exec -n drill wi-test -- sh -c 'curl -s -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google" "http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token"'
  # now returns a real {"access_token":"...","expires_in":...,"token_type":"Bearer"} — fixed

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code:
kubectl delete namespace drill
gcloud iam service-accounts delete drill-gsa@terraform-gke-learning.iam.gserviceaccount.com --project=terraform-gke-learning --quiet

problems.title: App calls the Kubernetes API itself and gets 403 — pure in-cluster RBAC, no GCP involved
problems.symptom: The 'controller' pod in drill runs code that lists other pods in its namespace via the Kubernetes API (a common pattern for operators/controllers). It fails with a 403. This has nothing to do with GCP or Workload Identity — the app never calls any Google API at all.
problems.hint: This is a completely different permission system from the Workload Identity drill — no GCP, no IAM, no GSA. It's asking whether the pod's own Kubernetes ServiceAccount has been granted any permission to talk to the Kubernetes API server itself.
problems.diagnosis: App logs show: 'pods is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:drill:controller-sa" cannot list resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "drill"'. kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:controller-sa -n drill -> 'no'. get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -n drill -> nothing binds controller-sa to any Role granting pod access.
problems.rootCause: Every ServiceAccount starts with effectively zero Kubernetes API permissions beyond what's explicitly granted via a RoleBinding (or ClusterRoleBinding) to a Role/ClusterRole. Nobody ever created a Role granting 'list pods' and bound it to controller-sa, so the API server correctly rejects the request — this is standard, intentional Kubernetes RBAC, working exactly as designed against an under-provisioned ServiceAccount, not a bug or a networking issue.
problems.fix: Create a Role scoped to exactly what the controller needs (get/list/watch on pods, in this namespace) and a RoleBinding attaching it to controller-sa — the principle of least privilege means granting only the specific verbs/resources actually used, not a broad catch-all.
problems.mental: 'kubectl auth can-i --as=<identity>' is the single fastest way to confirm/reproduce an RBAC permission gap before touching anything — it answers the exact yes/no question without needing to trigger the real app code path at all. Keep this fully separate in your head from GCP/Workload Identity: this drill's failure and fix never leave the Kubernetes API server; nothing here involves gcloud, GSAs, or IAM bindings.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create serviceaccount controller-sa
kubectl -n drill run controller --image=bitnami/kubectl --restart=Never --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"controller-sa"}}' -- sleep 3600
# no Role/RoleBinding created for controller-sa yet

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:controller-sa -n drill   # no
kubectl exec -n drill controller -- kubectl get pods -n drill                          # Error: pods is forbidden ... User "system:serviceaccount:drill:controller-sa" cannot list resource

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl -n drill create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl -n drill create rolebinding controller-pod-reader --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=drill:controller-sa
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:controller-sa -n drill   # yes
kubectl exec -n drill controller -- kubectl get pods -n drill                          # succeeds now

commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Bound correctly, still forbidden — a Role can't grant cluster-scoped access
problems.symptom: The 'auditor' ServiceAccount in drill has a RoleBinding that everyone swears grants it read access. Namespaced reads work fine. But the exact same identity gets 403 the moment it tries to list nodes — a cluster-scoped resource.
problems.hint: A Role and a ClusterRole can define the identical set of verbs and resources and still behave completely differently, depending on what KIND of resource is being accessed and what KIND of binding was used. Check whether the resource itself is namespaced or cluster-scoped.
problems.diagnosis: kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:auditor-sa -n drill -> yes. kubectl auth can-i get nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:auditor-sa -> no. describe rolebinding auditor-reader -n drill -> binds a Role (not ClusterRole) named 'reader' which itself includes a 'nodes' rule — but nodes is a cluster-scoped resource, and a Role (as opposed to a ClusterRole) can only ever grant access to resources WITHIN its own namespace, regardless of what verbs/resources are listed in its rules.
problems.rootCause: Nodes (like Namespaces, PersistentVolumes, and ClusterRoles themselves) are cluster-scoped resources — they don't belong to any namespace. A Role is inherently namespace-scoped: even if its rules literally list 'nodes' as a resource, a RoleBinding using that Role can never grant access to a cluster-scoped resource, because the Role's authority is capped at its own namespace by definition. The rule silently has zero effect for cluster-scoped resources rather than erroring at creation time, which is exactly what makes this so easy to miss.
problems.fix: Move the nodes rule into an actual ClusterRole, and grant it via a ClusterRoleBinding (for genuinely cluster-wide access) — or, if this identity should only see nodes-related info in some more limited way, reconsider whether it needs cluster-scoped access at all. There is no Role/RoleBinding combination that will ever grant access to a cluster-scoped resource, no matter how the rules are written.
problems.mental: Role/RoleBinding vs ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding is fundamentally about resource SCOPE, not just 'namespaced vs broader convenience' — a Role with a rule for a cluster-scoped resource type isn't a soft restriction, it's a no-op for that rule. Before writing any RBAC rule, know whether the target resource is namespaced (pods, deployments, secrets, configmaps, roles) or cluster-scoped (nodes, namespaces, persistentvolumes, clusterroles) — 'kubectl api-resources' has a NAMESPACED column that answers this directly.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create serviceaccount auditor-sa
kubectl -n drill create role reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods,nodes   # nodes rule here does nothing — Role is namespace-scoped
kubectl -n drill create rolebinding auditor-reader --role=reader --serviceaccount=drill:auditor-sa

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:auditor-sa -n drill    # yes
kubectl auth can-i get nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:auditor-sa            # no — despite 'nodes' being listed in the Role
kubectl api-resources | grep -E '^nodes '                                          # NAMESPACED column confirms nodes is cluster-scoped

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl create clusterrole node-reader --verb=get,list --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding auditor-node-reader --clusterrole=node-reader --serviceaccount=drill:auditor-sa
kubectl auth can-i get nodes --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:auditor-sa            # yes now

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code:
kubectl delete namespace drill
kubectl delete clusterrole node-reader
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding auditor-node-reader

problems.title: The RoleBinding exists and looks right — but names a ServiceAccount in the wrong namespace
problems.symptom: The 'exporter' ServiceAccount in drill is still getting 403 on an action a RoleBinding was specifically created to allow. 'kubectl get rolebinding' shows the binding exists, and 'kubectl describe' shows what looks like the right Role and the right ServiceAccount name.
problems.hint: A RoleBinding's subject for a ServiceAccount needs BOTH a name AND a namespace to uniquely identify who it's granting access to. Read the subject's namespace field specifically, not just the ServiceAccount name.
problems.diagnosis: describe rolebinding exporter-binding -n drill -> Subjects: Kind: ServiceAccount, Name: exporter-sa, Namespace: default. But 'kubectl get sa exporter-sa -n drill' shows the REAL ServiceAccount actually lives in drill, not default — a ServiceAccount named exporter-sa also happens to exist in default (a coincidence, or a copy-pasted manifest), and the binding is granting access to THAT one instead.
problems.rootCause: A RoleBinding's ServiceAccount subject is identified by the pair (name, namespace) together — 'exporter-sa' alone is not globally unique across the cluster; the same name can exist independently in every namespace. The binding was written with namespace: default (likely copy-pasted from a template or another environment) instead of namespace: drill, so it's silently granting the Role to a completely different, unrelated exporter-sa that happens to live in default, while the pod's REAL identity (drill's exporter-sa) gets nothing.
problems.fix: Correct the subject's namespace field in the RoleBinding to match where the ServiceAccount actually lives (drill). Since RoleBindings are immutable in their subjects/roleRef in practice (easiest to just delete and recreate), rebuild it with the right namespace rather than trying to patch a single field.
problems.mental: Never eyeball an RBAC subject by name alone — always check the (kind, name, namespace) triple together. Two ServiceAccounts with the identical name in different namespaces are completely unrelated identities to the API server; a RoleBinding pointing at the wrong one produces zero errors at creation time and looks entirely correct on a quick read, which is exactly why this is easy to ship.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create serviceaccount exporter-sa
kubectl -n default create serviceaccount exporter-sa   # unrelated SA, same name, different namespace
kubectl -n drill create role metrics-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: exporter-binding
  namespace: drill
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: exporter-sa
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: metrics-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:exporter-sa -n drill      # no — the real identity got nothing
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:exporter-sa -n drill    # yes — the WRONG one got the grant
kubectl describe rolebinding exporter-binding -n drill                                 # Subjects: Namespace: default

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl delete rolebinding exporter-binding -n drill
kubectl -n drill create rolebinding exporter-binding --role=metrics-reader --serviceaccount=drill:exporter-sa
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:drill:exporter-sa -n drill      # yes now

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code:
kubectl delete namespace drill
kubectl delete serviceaccount exporter-sa -n default

data.name: Storage & PersistentVolumeClaims
data.desc: A PVC and the pod using it are both stuck Pending — nothing crashed, nothing errored loudly, but nothing ever binds either. The answer lives in the PVC's own Events, and in whether the requested access mode is something the underlying storage type can physically provide.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA, IN PLAIN WORDS — a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a REQUEST for storage; it only becomes real
once something (a StorageClass's provisioner) actually creates a matching disk. Two ways that request
can be impossible to satisfy, both of which look identical at first glance (PVC stuck Pending):
  1. Typo'd/nonexistent StorageClass name -> nothing can ever provision, because nothing knows how.
  2. A REAL StorageClass, but an access mode it doesn't support -> provisioning is attempted and
     explicitly REJECTED, not just delayed.

ACCESS MODES, IN PLAIN WORDS:
  ReadWriteOnce (RWO)  -> one node at a time can mount it for read/write. This is what a normal disk
                          (GCE Persistent Disk) is — physically, a block device attached to one VM.
  ReadWriteMany (RWX)  -> many pods, potentially on many different nodes, mount and write at once.
                          Regular Persistent Disks CANNOT do this — it needs a real network filesystem
                          (e.g. Filestore-backed storage), a fundamentally different technology.
  Asking a Persistent-Disk-backed StorageClass for RWX isn't a config mistake Kubernetes can silently
  work around — it's asking a single-attach block device to behave like a shared network drive.

WHY THE FAILURE IS DELAYED (CONFIRMED IN PRACTICE): the default StorageClass uses 'WaitForFirstConsumer'
binding mode — Kubernetes deliberately provisions NOTHING until a pod that actually uses the PVC gets
scheduled (Events: 'WaitForFirstConsumer' -> 'WaitForPodScheduled'). Only once a pod is scheduled does
the CSI driver's CreateVolume call run — and THAT's the exact moment an impossible request gets
rejected: 'ProvisioningFailed ... VolumeCapabilities is invalid: specified multi writer with mount
access type' (the driver's technical name for ReadWriteMany). This delay is why the PVC can sit
looking merely 'not bound yet' for a while before the real, permanent error ever appears.

BONUS FINDING: patching a running Deployment to add a volume creates a NEW ReplicaSet (new pod that
needs the volume) while the OLD ReplicaSet's pod (no volume, already healthy) stays put, since the
rollout can't proceed until the new pod becomes Ready. A storage problem can therefore masquerade as a
'stuck rollout' — 'kubectl get pods' showing two pods, one Running one Pending, is the tell.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: A PVC is stuck Pending — what's the very first thing you check?
A: 'kubectl describe pvc' and read its Events, not just its Status. The Events say exactly which stage
   it's stuck at — waiting for a consumer, waiting for the provisioner, or an outright rejected request.

Q: Why would a PVC sit fine for a while and only fail once a pod is actually scheduled?
A: 'WaitForFirstConsumer' binding mode delays provisioning until a consuming pod is scheduled (so the
   disk gets created in the right zone). Nothing is validated before that point — including whether the
   requested access mode is even possible.

Q: Can you ever get ReadWriteMany on GKE?
A: Not with a regular Persistent-Disk-backed StorageClass. You need storage built for concurrent
   multi-node access — e.g. a Filestore-backed StorageClass (NFS) — a different underlying technology,
   not a config tweak on the same disk type.

problems.title: PVC and pod both stuck Pending — ReadWriteMany on a disk that can't do it
problems.symptom: The 'storage-app' deployment in drill needs a shared data volume — the plan was for multiple replicas to read/write the same disk simultaneously. 'kubectl get pods' shows it stuck Pending. 'kubectl get pvc' shows the claim also stuck Pending. Nothing crashed — nothing ever started. What's actually blocking this, and can it ever resolve on its own?
problems.hint: Not every kind of storage supports being attached to multiple pods writing at once — the access mode you request has to be something the underlying storage type can physically provide. Check the PVC's own Events, not just its Status.
problems.diagnosis: describe pvc shared-data -> Events show a sequence: 'WaitForFirstConsumer' (normal, just waiting for a pod) -> 'WaitForPodScheduled' -> 'Provisioning' -> then 'ProvisioningFailed: Volume provisioning failed with infeasible error ... rpc error: code = InvalidArgument desc = VolumeCapabilities is invalid: specified multi writer with mount access type'. get pods shows TWO pods: the original one (Running, from before the volume was added) and a new one (Pending, from after) — the rollout is stuck because the new pod can never satisfy its volume dependency.
problems.rootCause: The PVC requested accessModes: ["ReadWriteMany"] against storageClassName: standard-rwo, which is backed by the pd.csi.storage.gke.io provisioner — a regular GCE Persistent Disk. A Persistent Disk is a block device that can only be attached for read/write to ONE node at a time; ReadWriteMany explicitly asks for many nodes to mount and write simultaneously, which this storage type is physically incapable of providing, not just unconfigured for. Because binding mode is WaitForFirstConsumer, this impossibility isn't caught until a pod actually gets scheduled and the CSI driver's CreateVolume call runs — before that point, the PVC just looks like it's 'waiting,' not broken.
problems.fix: Change the access mode to ReadWriteOnce, matching what Persistent Disk actually supports. If genuine multi-pod concurrent read/write access is a real requirement, the fix isn't a different accessMode value on the same StorageClass — it requires a StorageClass backed by a filesystem built for that (e.g. Filestore/NFS-backed), a different storage technology entirely.
problems.mental: A PVC stuck Pending has (at least) two distinct root causes that look identical at first: a StorageClass that doesn't exist (nothing can ever provision — permanently stuck immediately) versus a real StorageClass asked for something it can't do (provisioning is attempted and explicitly rejected, but only once a pod triggers it, thanks to WaitForFirstConsumer). Always read the PVC's Events in full, in order — the sequence itself tells you which stage you're stuck at. And remember: a volume problem can disguise itself as a stuck rollout — two pods, one healthy and old, one Pending and new, is the giveaway.

problems.title: PVC stuck Pending from the first second — nothing can ever provision it
problems.symptom: The 'media' pod in drill has been Pending since the moment it was applied — no delay, no partial progress, immediately stuck. Its PVC shows the same: Pending from the very first check.
problems.hint: Compare this timing against the RWX drill: that one looked fine for a while before failing, because binding mode waits for a consuming pod. If THIS one never even gets that far, the problem is earlier — something the PVC references may not exist at all.
problems.diagnosis: describe pvc media-data -n drill -> Events: 'no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set' / 'storageclass.storage.k8s.io "standard-rwo-typo" not found'. get storageclass -> confirms no StorageClass exists under that exact name — 'standard-rwo' (no suffix) is what's actually available.
problems.rootCause: The PVC's storageClassName references a StorageClass name that was never created ('standard-rwo-typo' vs the real 'standard-rwo') — a straightforward typo. Unlike the RWX access-mode drill, where a REAL StorageClass exists but rejects an impossible request only once a pod triggers provisioning, this fails immediately and permanently: there is no provisioner to even attempt binding, so there's no WaitForFirstConsumer delay to mask it — Pending here means stuck from second one.
problems.fix: Correct the storageClassName to the real StorageClass name, or omit it entirely to use whatever StorageClass is marked default in the cluster (check with 'kubectl get storageclass' — the default has an '(default)' annotation).
problems.mental: Two flavors of 'PVC can never bind,' distinguished by timing: a nonexistent StorageClass name fails immediately, permanently, with no waiting period at all — there's nothing to attempt. An access-mode mismatch against a REAL StorageClass can look fine for a while (WaitForFirstConsumer) before failing only once a pod is scheduled. If a PVC has been stuck since the literal instant it was created, check the StorageClass NAME first, before assuming anything about access modes.

problems.title: PVC is Bound, pod is ContainerCreating forever — a subPath that doesn't exist in the volume
problems.symptom: The 'archive' pod in drill sits in ContainerCreating far longer than any image pull should take. Its PVC shows Bound — storage itself isn't the problem, at least not obviously.
problems.hint: ContainerCreating that never resolves, with a Bound PVC, points at the MOUNT step specifically rather than provisioning. Check Events for a message about the volume mount itself, not the PVC's binding status.
problems.diagnosis: get pvc -> Bound, looks completely fine. get pods -> stuck ContainerCreating, past when an image pull would normally finish. describe pod -> Events: 'MountVolume.SetUp failed ... subPath "logs" not found'. The volume mount specifies subPath: logs, but nothing ever created a 'logs' subdirectory inside the underlying volume before the pod tried to mount it.
problems.rootCause: A subPath mount requires that path to already exist WITHIN the volume before the container can be created — unlike a plain root-of-volume mount (which just uses the volume's root, always 'exists' trivially), kubelet does not auto-create missing subPath directories inside an already-provisioned PVC. Since 'logs' was never created inside this fresh volume, the mount step itself fails repeatedly, blocking the container from ever starting, even though the PVC and StorageClass layers are both completely healthy.
problems.fix: Either remove the subPath and mount the volume's root instead (simplest, if nothing else needs to share that volume), or pre-populate the expected subdirectory — commonly via an initContainer that runs 'mkdir -p' against the same volume before the main container's subPath mount is attempted.
problems.mental: 'PVC Bound + pod stuck ContainerCreating' isolates the failure to the MOUNT step specifically, separate from every provisioning-layer PVC drill (Pending PVC, wrong StorageClass, impossible access mode) — those all fail before a PVC even reaches Bound. subPath referencing a path that doesn't yet exist inside the volume is one of the most common ContainerCreating-forever causes once the PVC itself is healthy; the fix is almost always either drop subPath or pre-create the path with an initContainer.

problems.title: Deleted the pod, deleted the PVC — the disk is still there and still billing
problems.symptom: After tearing down a test StatefulSet in drill and deleting its PVCs, someone notices the underlying GCE Persistent Disks are STILL showing up in 'gcloud compute disks list' — nothing was actually freed.
problems.hint: Deleting a PVC doesn't automatically mean the underlying disk gets deleted — what happens to the real disk when its claim goes away is a separate, explicit setting on the PersistentVolume itself.
problems.diagnosis: get pv -> a PV shows STATUS: Released (not Deleted, not Available) — its old claimRef still points at the now-gone PVC, and it can't be reused by a new claim in this state. describe pv -> Reclaim Policy: Retain. gcloud compute disks list -> the backing disk is still present and still incurring cost, exactly as Retain is designed to do.
problems.rootCause: The StorageClass this PV was provisioned from has reclaimPolicy: Retain, which deliberately preserves the underlying disk (and the PV object, in a Released state) after its PVC is deleted — a safety choice for data some teams don't want auto-deleted. This is working as configured, not a bug, but it means 'delete the PVC' does NOT mean 'delete the disk' the way it would under the more common reclaimPolicy: Delete default, and a Released PV sits unusable until manually handled.
problems.fix: If the data genuinely doesn't need to be kept, manually delete both the PV object and the underlying disk ('kubectl delete pv' then 'gcloud compute disks delete'). If Retain was chosen deliberately for safety, that's correct behavior — but the team needs a documented process for actually cleaning up Released PVs and their disks, since nothing does it automatically, ever.
problems.mental: reclaimPolicy is the single field that determines what 'delete the PVC' actually does to the real disk underneath it — Delete (default on most GKE StorageClasses) removes the disk automatically; Retain leaves both the disk and a Released PV behind, permanently, until someone does that cleanup by hand. Always check reclaimPolicy before assuming 'delete PVC' equals 'stop paying for the disk' — this is exactly the kind of gap that shows up as an unexplained GCP bill line item.

problems.title: Replaced the StatefulSet, the new pod inherited the OLD pod's disk — on purpose
problems.symptom: A StatefulSet pod ('web-db-0') in drill was deleted to force a fresh restart after a bad state. The new pod that came back up still has all the old data on its volume — nobody expected that, since a Deployment's pods are normally treated as fully disposable.
problems.hint: StatefulSets manage storage fundamentally differently from Deployments — the identity 'web-db-0' specifically is tied to a specific PVC, not just a pod name pattern. Check whether that PVC was actually recreated, or just reattached.
problems.diagnosis: get pvc -n drill -l app=web-db -> a PVC named 'data-web-db-0' still exists, unchanged, from before the pod deletion. get pods -n drill -> the new web-db-0 pod mounts that SAME PVC — same name, same volumeHandle, same disk, same data. This is not a coincidence or a caching bug.
problems.rootCause: A StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates create ONE PVC PER ORDINAL (data-web-db-0, data-web-db-1, ...) that persists independently of the pod's own lifecycle — deleting the POD does not delete its PVC. When the StatefulSet controller recreates web-db-0, it deterministically reattaches to the PVC already named for that ordinal, by design, so a replica keeps its own durable identity and data across restarts/rescheduling — this is the entire point of using a StatefulSet over a Deployment for stateful workloads.
problems.fix: Nothing to 'fix' here if this was actually the desired behavior — this IS how StatefulSets are supposed to work. If the intent really was a clean wipe, the PVC has to be deleted EXPLICITLY and separately from the pod ('kubectl delete pvc data-web-db-0'), which then forces a brand-new disk to be provisioned the next time that ordinal's pod starts.
problems.mental: This is the flip side of a bug — the surprise here comes from applying Deployment mental models (pods are disposable, nothing persists) to a StatefulSet, where PER-REPLICA STORAGE IS THE ENTIRE FEATURE. Deleting a StatefulSet pod is a restart of that specific numbered identity, not a fresh instance; deleting the StatefulSet itself ALSO doesn't delete its PVCs by default (they outlive the StatefulSet on purpose too) — genuinely wiping data always requires an explicit, separate PVC deletion.

kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: web-db, namespace: drill }
spec:
  serviceName: web-db
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web-db } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web-db } }
    spec:

        volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /data }]

kubectl wait -n drill --for=condition=Ready pod/web-db-0 --timeout=120s

data.name: Node-Level Pressure & Evictions
data.desc: A pod just disappears — no crash loop, no OOM in the usual sense, RESTARTS often still shows 0. It was Evicted: kubelet actively removed it to protect the node from running out of a resource. On Autopilot there's no node shell access, so this shows up and is drilled at the POD's own resource-limit level instead of true node administration.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA, IN PLAIN WORDS — Evicted is NOT the same failure family as CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled, even
though it can look similar at a glance (pod gone, Exit Code 137 again). CrashLoopBackOff/OOMKilled are
the CONTAINER failing on its own. Evicted is kubelet PROACTIVELY removing a healthy, still-running pod
to protect the node (or, for a per-container ephemeral-storage limit, to protect the limit itself) —
the pod didn't fail by itself, it got removed from outside.

WHY THIS IS DRILLED DIFFERENTLY ON AUTOPILOT: Google manages Autopilot's nodes directly — no SSH/exec
access, no way to safely force real node-wide disk pressure without risking other tenants' workloads on
a shared node. What Autopilot DOES let you control directly is a container's own ephemeral-storage
LIMIT — and kubelet enforces that exactly the same way it would enforce true node-level disk pressure,
just scoped to one pod. It's also the more common REAL version of this incident anyway: a single
runaway container filling up local disk, not the whole node being genuinely out of space.

CONFIRMED IN PRACTICE (drill): a container with 'resources.limits.ephemeral-storage: 1Gi' wrote ~1.95GiB
into a plain emptyDir volume (no SizeLimit of its own, so it counts fully against the container's
ephemeral-storage limit). Result: 'kubectl get pods' showed a confusing 'ContainerStatusUnknown' status
— NOT the word 'Evicted' — the real reason only appears in 'kubectl describe', in the top-level Reason
field: 'Reason: Evicted, Message: Pod ephemeral local storage usage exceeds the total limit of
containers 1Gi.' Exit Code on the container was 137 — SAME code as OOMKilled and a liveness-probe kill
from earlier drills. Three different causes, one signal, yet again — 137 just means SIGKILL, full stop.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: A pod disappears, RESTARTS is 0, Exit Code is 137 — is that always OOMKilled?
A: No — confirmed three separate times now: OOMKilled (memory), a liveness-probe-triggered kill, and
   ephemeral-storage eviction all produce Exit Code 137, because 137 only encodes SIGKILL, not why.
   Always check describe's Reason field (OOMKilled vs Evicted) and Events, never stop at the exit code.

Q: 'kubectl get pods' shows STATUS ContainerStatusUnknown — what does that actually mean?
A: It usually means the container was forcibly removed (evicted, or its node/runtime lost track of it)
   before the kubelet could report a clean terminal status. It is NOT a useful diagnosis on its own —
   go straight to 'kubectl describe pod' and read the top-level Reason and Message fields.

Q: A pod got Evicted for ephemeral-storage — do you just raise the limit?
A: Same judgment call as OOMKilled: if the usage is real and expected, raise the limit with headroom
   (confirmed, not guessed). If it's unbounded — a log file that's never rotated, a temp-file leak —
   raising the limit only buys time before the identical eviction happens again at a higher number.

problems.title: Pod vanishes, RESTARTS still 0 — ephemeral-storage eviction
problems.symptom: The 'disk-hog' pod in drill was running fine a minute ago. Now 'kubectl get pods' shows it gone from Running — status says something else entirely. It wasn't OOMKilled, it wasn't CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS is still 0. What actually happened to it?
problems.hint: This isn't a memory problem and it isn't a crash. Something is enforcing a different resource limit entirely — and once it's tripped, the pod doesn't restart, it's gone for good under that name.
problems.diagnosis: get pods -> STATUS shows 'ContainerStatusUnknown', not an obviously useful label. describe pod -> the real answer is at the TOP, not in the container block: 'Status: Failed, Reason: Evicted, Message: Pod ephemeral local storage usage exceeds the total limit of containers 1Gi.' Events confirm: 'Warning Evicted ... exceeds the total limit of containers 1Gi' followed by 'Normal Killing ... Stopping container disk-hog'. Container's Exit Code shows 137 — same SIGKILL code as OOMKilled, misleading if read in isolation.
problems.rootCause: The container's resources.limits.ephemeral-storage was set to 1Gi, but its command ('dd if=/dev/zero of=/data/bigfile bs=1M count=2000') wrote roughly 1.95GiB into a plain emptyDir volume mounted at /data. A plain emptyDir with no SizeLimit of its own counts fully against the container's ephemeral-storage limit, so total local-disk usage blew well past the 1Gi ceiling. kubelet's eviction manager actively monitors this and killed the pod specifically to enforce that limit — this is intentional protective behavior, not a bug or a crash.
problems.fix: If ~2GB of scratch space is genuinely expected usage, raise the ephemeral-storage limit to comfortably cover it (with headroom, same principle as sizing a memory limit). If the usage is actually unbounded — an app writing logs or temp files without ever cleaning them up — raising the limit only delays the identical eviction at a higher threshold; fix what's writing the data instead.
problems.mental: Evicted is a different failure family from CrashLoopBackOff/OOMKilled — the container didn't fail on its own, kubelet proactively removed a still-healthy pod to protect a resource limit. The tell in 'kubectl get pods' is often a vague status like ContainerStatusUnknown, not the word 'Evicted' itself — always confirm with 'kubectl describe pod' and read the top-level Reason/Message fields, not just the container's exit code. And once again: Exit Code 137 by itself proves nothing beyond 'something sent SIGKILL' — OOM, a failed liveness probe, and ephemeral-storage eviction all produce the identical code.

problems.title: Pods evicted off a node that's suddenly NotReady
problems.symptom: Every pod that was on a specific node in the cluster shows up rescheduled elsewhere within the last few minutes — no CrashLoop, no OOM, no eviction message about disk or memory limits on any individual pod. The common thread is which NODE they used to be on.
problems.hint: When the pods themselves all look fine individually but they're all fleeing the SAME node at the SAME time, stop looking at pod specs entirely and go look at the node's own Conditions.
problems.diagnosis: get nodes -> one node shows STATUS: NotReady. describe node <name> -> Conditions: Ready = Unknown/False, with a LastHeartbeatTime that stopped updating. get pods -A -o wide (filtered to that former node) -> shows nothing now — everything already moved. get events -A --field-selector involvedObject.kind=Node -> 'NodeNotReady' followed by pods being marked for eviction after tolerationSeconds elapsed.
problems.rootCause: kubelet on that node stopped reporting healthy status to the control plane (in real incidents: a kubelet crash, a node-level network partition, or the VM itself becoming unresponsive). Every pod schedules with an implicit toleration for the 'node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoExecute' taint with a default tolerationSeconds (300s) — once the node is marked NotReady and stays that way past that window, the control plane taints it and evicts every pod that didn't explicitly tolerate the condition longer, rescheduling them elsewhere. On GKE Autopilot, Google's own node auto-repair typically kicks in to replace the unhealthy node automatically.
problems.fix: On Autopilot, this is usually self-healing — GKE's node auto-repair detects and replaces the unhealthy node without any manual action; confirm via 'gcloud container operations list' that a repair operation ran. On Standard GKE (or if auto-repair is disabled), the on-call action is to investigate the VM itself (serial console logs, underlying compute instance health) rather than anything at the Kubernetes layer — the affected pods have already been correctly handled by the scheduler moving them elsewhere.
problems.mental: NotReady is a NODE-level Condition, not a pod-level failure signature — it explains a whole batch of otherwise-unrelated pods all moving at once, which no single-pod diagnostic (logs, describe pod, exit codes) will ever surface on its own. 'kubectl get nodes' + describe node's Conditions block is the starting point whenever multiple, otherwise-healthy-looking pods move simultaneously. On managed Autopilot nodes there's no SSH access to genuinely crash a kubelet for practice — the taint below is applied manually here to reproduce the CONSEQUENCE (the eviction mechanics) safely, without needing real node failure.

commands.label: Setup — simulate the consequence safely (no real node crash on managed Autopilot)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create deployment sensor --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1
kubectl wait -n drill --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=sensor --timeout=60s
NODE=$(kubectl get pod -n drill -l app=sensor -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.nodeName}')
# apply the SAME taint the control plane applies to a real NotReady node:
kubectl taint node $NODE node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoExecute --overwrite

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill -w                                  # watch it get evicted and rescheduled elsewhere after tolerationSeconds
kubectl get events -n drill --sort-by=.lastTimestamp           # eviction event tied to the NoExecute taint
kubectl describe node $NODE | grep Taints                      # confirms the simulated NotReady taint is present

commands.label: Cleanup (remove the simulated taint, real incidents self-heal via auto-repair)
commands.code:
kubectl taint node $NODE node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoExecute-
kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Multiple unrelated pods evicted at once — genuine node-level DiskPressure
problems.symptom: Several DIFFERENT pods, belonging to different Deployments, all got evicted from the same node within seconds of each other. None of them individually had an ephemeral-storage limit set — this looks nothing like the earlier per-container eviction drill.
problems.hint: When pods with completely unrelated specs — no shared limit, no shared image — get evicted together, the trigger isn't inside any one of their container specs. It's a property of the NODE they all happened to share.
problems.diagnosis: describe node <name> -> Conditions include 'DiskPressure: True'. get events -A --field-selector reason=Evicted -> multiple pods, different apps, same node, same timestamp window, each Message reading 'The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage'. Unlike the earlier drill's per-container 'exceeds the total limit of containers 1Gi' wording, this message names the NODE as being low on the resource, not any single container's own limit.
problems.rootCause: Total disk usage across ALL pods (plus images, logs, and system overhead) on that node crossed kubelet's node-level eviction threshold — a genuine, real capacity problem at the node, not any individual pod's ephemeral-storage LIMIT being exceeded. kubelet's eviction manager responds by evicting pods to bring the node back under threshold, generally starting with the pods furthest over their own requests, regardless of which app they belong to — which is why unrelated workloads get caught in the same sweep.
problems.fix: Identify what's actually consuming node disk in aggregate — often unbounded container logs, unpruned image layers, or many pods each writing modest but uncapped scratch data that adds up. Setting sensible per-container ephemeral-storage requests/limits (the earlier drill's fix) helps kubelet schedule and reason about disk budget per pod, but the durable node-level fix is usually addressing what's actually filling the disk (log rotation, image GC settings) rather than any single pod's spec.
problems.mental: Distinguish this from the earlier drill precisely by SCOPE: a per-container ephemeral-storage LIMIT being exceeded evicts exactly ONE pod, and Events name that specific container's limit. Genuine node-level DiskPressure can evict SEVERAL unrelated pods in the same window, and Events/describe node explicitly say the NODE is low on the resource, not any pod's own limit. On managed Autopilot nodes, actually filling real node disk to reproduce this safely (without risking other tenants on a shared node) isn't something to force live — recognizing the distinct signature (multiple unrelated pods, DiskPressure: True on the node) is the transferable skill here.

commands.label: Setup — recognize rather than force (real node disk fill is disruptive on shared Autopilot nodes)
commands.code:
# Genuinely filling a managed node's real disk risks other tenants sharing that node and isn't
# something to do casually, even on a personal learning cluster. Recognize the signature below
# instead of reproducing actual DiskPressure live.

commands.label: Diagnose (what it looks like when it happens for real)
commands.code:
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -A5 Conditions        # DiskPressure: True
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=Evicted --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
  # multiple different pods, same node, same window, Message: 'node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage'
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TAINTS:.spec.taints   # look for node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure:NoSchedule

commands.label: Fix / prevention
commands.code:
# per-pod: give every container a sane ephemeral-storage request/limit so kubelet can budget disk per pod
# node-level: check what's actually consuming disk in aggregate
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_node" AND jsonPayload.message:"disk"' --limit=20 --project=terraform-gke-learning
# and confirm log rotation / image garbage collection settings are sane rather than unbounded

data.name: Resource Quotas & LimitRanges
data.desc: A pod is never even created — no Pending, no CrashLoopBackOff, no Events on any pod object at all, because no pod object exists. The API server rejected the request outright at admission time, before anything Kubernetes-schedulable was ever produced. The answer lives in namespace-level policy, not in anything pod-shaped.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA — ResourceQuota and LimitRange are BOTH namespace-level admission-time controls, but they do
completely different jobs and fail completely differently:
  • ResourceQuota  -> caps the TOTAL sum of something across the whole namespace (total CPU requested,
    total pod count, total PVC count...). Once the sum is already at the cap, the NEXT object that would
    push it over gets flatly REJECTED at creation — 'kubectl apply'/'create' itself errors out immediately,
    with no object of any kind ever getting created. There's nothing to describe or debug on a pod,
    because no pod was ever made.
  • LimitRange     -> sets DEFAULTS and per-object MIN/MAX bounds for individual pods/containers in a
    namespace (e.g. every container gets a default 100m CPU request if it doesn't specify one; nothing
    can request more than 2 CPU). It can also REJECT creation if a pod's own explicit request falls
    outside the allowed min/max — same instant admission-time rejection, different reason entirely.

THE TELL: the error surfaces immediately on the 'kubectl apply'/'create' COMMAND LINE ITSELF, not later
via 'kubectl describe pod' — because there's no pod object in existence to describe. This is fundamentally
different from every Pending/CrashLoop/Evicted drill in this vault, where SOMETHING got created first and
then failed. Quota/LimitRange rejections happen at the door, before the object exists at all.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: A 'kubectl apply' for a Deployment succeeds, but zero of its pods ever appear — not even Pending. Why?
A: The Deployment/ReplicaSet objects themselves can still be created even if pod creation is blocked by a
   ResourceQuota — check 'kubectl describe replicaset' for a FailedCreate event citing 'exceeded quota',
   and 'kubectl describe resourcequota -n <ns>' to see exactly which dimension (pods, cpu, requests.memory)
   is already maxed out.

Q: What's the practical difference between what ResourceQuota and LimitRange each control?
A: ResourceQuota caps the TOTAL across the whole namespace (namespace-wide budget). LimitRange sets
   PER-CONTAINER/PER-POD defaults and min/max bounds (individual object shape). A namespace commonly has
   both — LimitRange keeps individual pods sane, ResourceQuota keeps the aggregate in check.

Q: A pod's creation is rejected citing a LimitRange, even though the manifest looks completely normal —
   what's the first thing to check?
A: Whether the pod's own explicit resources.requests/limits fall within that namespace's LimitRange
   min/max bounds — 'kubectl describe limitrange -n <ns>' shows the exact allowed range per resource type.

problems.title: Deployment applies fine, replicas never appear — ResourceQuota exceeded
problems.symptom: 'kubectl apply' on the 'ingest' Deployment in drill returns success with no error. But 'kubectl get pods' shows nothing — not Pending, not any status at all. Zero pods exist for it, and nothing in the Deployment's own describe output looks obviously wrong.
problems.hint: The Deployment and ReplicaSet objects themselves got created fine — the apply DID succeed. So the block is happening one layer down, at the point where the ReplicaSet tries to actually create pod objects. Check the ReplicaSet's own Events, and check what limits this namespace has.
problems.diagnosis: get deployment,rs -n drill -> both exist. describe rs (the ReplicaSet backing ingest) -> Events: 'FailedCreate: Error creating: pods "ingest-xxxxx" is forbidden: exceeded quota: drill-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=10, limited: pods=10'. get resourcequota drill-quota -n drill -> confirms pods 10/10, already fully consumed by other workloads in the namespace.
problems.rootCause: A ResourceQuota (drill-quota) caps the total pod COUNT in this namespace at 10, and other workloads already consume all 10 slots. The Deployment and ReplicaSet objects are cluster-API-level objects that ARE allowed to be created regardless of quota — quota enforcement happens specifically at POD creation, which is why 'kubectl apply' itself reports success (it only created the Deployment/ReplicaSet) while the actual pods silently never materialize, with the real rejection recorded only on the ReplicaSet's Events, one layer removed from what most people check first.
problems.fix: Either free up quota headroom (scale down or clean up unused workloads elsewhere in the namespace) or raise the ResourceQuota's pod limit if the higher pod count is genuinely needed and approved. No changes to the Deployment itself are needed — once quota headroom exists, the ReplicaSet controller automatically retries pod creation with no further action.
problems.mental: This is the one failure family in the whole vault where the TOP-LEVEL object (Deployment) succeeds outright and the real rejection is buried on a DIFFERENT object's Events (the ReplicaSet) — 'kubectl describe' on the thing you applied often isn't where the answer is. Whenever a Deployment applies cleanly but produces zero pods with zero Pending status, check the ReplicaSet's Events and the namespace's ResourceQuota before assuming anything about the pod spec itself.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create quota drill-quota --hard=pods=10
# fill the quota with filler pods first:
kubectl -n drill create deployment filler --image=busybox --replicas=10 -- sleep 3600
kubectl wait -n drill --for=condition=Available deployment/filler --timeout=60s
# now try to add one more, unrelated, workload:
kubectl -n drill create deployment ingest --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill -l app=ingest                        # nothing — not even Pending
kubectl get rs -n drill -l app=ingest                          # the ReplicaSet DOES exist
kubectl describe rs -n drill -l app=ingest                     # Events: FailedCreate, exceeded quota
kubectl describe resourcequota drill-quota -n drill             # pods: 10/10 used

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl -n drill scale deployment filler --replicas=8            # free up 2 slots
kubectl get pods -n drill -l app=ingest -w                      # ReplicaSet retries automatically -> 1/1 Running

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: Pod creation rejected before it ever exists — LimitRange minimum not met
problems.symptom: Applying the 'scheduler-app' pod spec in drill fails IMMEDIATELY on the apply command itself — not Pending, not any kubectl get result at all, an outright error printed right there in the terminal.
problems.hint: An immediate rejection on the apply command, with no object created whatsoever, is admission-time enforcement — the same family as the quota drill, but the message text will point at a different mechanism this time.
problems.diagnosis: kubectl apply -f scheduler-app.yaml -> 'error: pods "scheduler-app" is forbidden: minimum cpu usage per Container is 100m, but request is 50m'. describe limitrange -n drill -> shows Type: Container, Min cpu: 100m — this namespace has a floor on how little CPU any single container is allowed to request.
problems.rootCause: A LimitRange in this namespace enforces a MINIMUM cpu request per container (100m) — set to stop severely under-provisioned containers from being scheduled, which can cause CPU starvation/throttling in practice. The pod's manifest explicitly requested 50m, below that floor, so the API server rejects the object at admission, before it's ever persisted — there is genuinely nothing to 'kubectl get' afterward, since creation itself never completed.
problems.fix: Raise the container's cpu request to at least the LimitRange's minimum (100m or higher, based on real expected usage — not just the bare minimum to get past the check). If 50m was actually sufficient for this specific workload, that's a signal the LimitRange's minimum may be miscalibrated for this namespace and worth a conversation with whoever owns it, rather than just padding every request to clear the bar.
problems.mental: LimitRange rejections and ResourceQuota rejections both happen at admission time with zero object created, but the deciding factor is different: ResourceQuota is about the NAMESPACE-WIDE total already being maxed out; LimitRange is about THIS ONE pod's own request falling outside a configured min/max, regardless of what anything else in the namespace is using. 'kubectl describe limitrange -n <ns>' shows the exact bounds in force.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: { name: drill-limits, namespace: drill }
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    min: { cpu: 100m }
    max: { cpu: 2 }
EOF

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: scheduler-app, namespace: drill }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: scheduler-app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    resources: { requests: { cpu: "50m" } }
EOF
# error: pods "scheduler-app" is forbidden: minimum cpu usage per Container is 100m, but request is 50m
kubectl describe limitrange drill-limits -n drill            # confirms the Min cpu: 100m bound

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

kind: Pod
metadata: { name: scheduler-app, namespace: drill }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: scheduler-app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    resources: { requests: { cpu: "150m" } }
EOF
kubectl get pods -n drill                                     # created successfully, 1/1 Running

data.name: Rollout & Deployment Strategy
data.desc: Nothing is crashing, nothing is Pending — the pods themselves are perfectly healthy. The problem lives in the ROLLOUT mechanics: how many old vs new pods are allowed to exist at once, and what happens when the 'new' version being rolled toward is itself broken.
data.notes:
KEY IDEA — a rolling update is governed by two numbers on the Deployment's strategy, and misreading either
one produces a stuck-looking rollout that has nothing to do with the application itself:
  • maxUnavailable  -> how many of the OLD, working replicas are allowed to be taken down before their
    NEW replacements are Ready. Too aggressive (a high number, or 100%) risks capacity during the rollout.
    Too conservative (0) can mean the rollout can't even start removing old pods until new ones catch up.
  • maxSurge         -> how many EXTRA pods (above the normal replica count) are allowed to exist
    temporarily while rolling out. If maxSurge is 0 AND maxUnavailable is also too small, there may not be
    enough 'room' for the rollout to make progress at all — especially combined with tight resource quotas.

THE TELL: 'kubectl rollout status' hangs indefinitely with no error, and 'kubectl get pods' shows a mix of
old and new ReplicaSet pods that never fully converges — not any individual pod being unhealthy.

ROLLBACK ISN'T ALWAYS A FIX: 'kubectl rollout undo' targets a specific PREVIOUS revision. If that revision
was itself broken (a bad revision got rolled forward earlier and only caught later), undo can roll you
straight back into the SAME failure — always check what a revision's image/config actually was
('kubectl rollout history --revision=N') before assuming undo is automatically safe.

COMMON INTERVIEW Qs
Q: A rollout seems permanently stuck — 'kubectl get pods' shows some old, some new, no progress for
   several minutes. Where do you look?
A: 'kubectl describe deployment' Conditions (look for ProgressDeadlineExceeded) and rollout strategy
   fields (maxUnavailable/maxSurge) together with 'kubectl get rs' to see how many pods each ReplicaSet
   actually has versus how many it wants.

Q: Is 'kubectl rollout undo' always safe?
A: No — it rolls back to a specific prior revision, which is only safe if THAT revision was actually
   healthy. Check 'kubectl rollout history' and the target revision's actual image/config before undoing,
   especially after multiple bad deploys in a row.

problems.title: Rollout stuck halfway forever — maxUnavailable: 0 with no room to surge
problems.symptom: The 'frontend' Deployment in drill (3 replicas) was updated with a new image ten minutes ago. 'kubectl rollout status' never returns. 'kubectl get pods' shows 2 old pods still Running and 1 new pod stuck Pending — no CrashLoop, no error on any individual pod.
problems.hint: Every individual pod here is healthy or normally-Pending on its own — the problem isn't inside any pod spec. It's about how many pods are allowed to exist AT ONCE during this specific rollout, combined with what capacity is actually available.
problems.diagnosis: describe deployment frontend -> strategy: RollingUpdate, maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1. get rs -n drill -> old ReplicaSet still has all 3 desired pods (maxUnavailable: 0 means Kubernetes won't remove any old pod until a new one is Ready), new ReplicaSet has 1 pod, Pending. describe that new pod -> FailedScheduling: Insufficient cpu — there's only enough spare cluster capacity for the surge pod IF resource requests were smaller than what's configured.
problems.rootCause: maxUnavailable: 0 means Kubernetes will never remove an old pod before a new one is Ready — correct for zero-downtime rollouts, but it means the ONLY way forward is via maxSurge (1 extra pod above the normal 3). That single surge pod can't get scheduled due to real resource constraints, so the rollout has no path to progress: it won't remove an old pod (maxUnavailable: 0 forbids it) and it can't add more than one extra pod (maxSurge: 1) to work around the stuck surge pod either. The rollout isn't failing — it's correctly waiting for a precondition that current cluster capacity can't satisfy.
problems.fix: Either free up capacity so the surge pod can actually schedule (same fix as any Pending-from-insufficient-resources drill), or temporarily raise maxSurge so more room exists to work with, or — if brief unavailability is acceptable for this specific rollout — allow a small maxUnavailable (e.g. 1) so an old pod can be retired to make room instead of depending entirely on surge capacity.
problems.mental: A rollout that hangs with mixed old/new pods and zero individual pod errors is a STRATEGY-level problem, not an app-level one — go straight to 'kubectl describe deployment' Conditions and the maxUnavailable/maxSurge values, cross-referenced against 'kubectl describe' on whichever new pod is stuck. The individual stuck pod's OWN reason (here, Insufficient cpu) is still the real root cause underneath — the rollout strategy is just what's making that one stuck pod block the ENTIRE deployment instead of only itself.

commands.label: Setup (break it)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: frontend, namespace: drill }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: frontend } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: frontend } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: nginx:alpine
        resources: { requests: { cpu: "200m" } }
EOF
kubectl rollout status deployment/frontend -n drill --timeout=60s
# now roll to a version whose surge pod requests far more cpu than the cluster has spare:
kubectl -n drill patch deployment frontend --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu","value":"16"},{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image","value":"nginx:1.27-alpine"}]'

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl rollout status deployment/frontend -n drill --timeout=15s   # never converges
kubectl get pods -n drill -o wide                                   # 2 old Running, 1 new Pending
kubectl get rs -n drill                                              # old RS still at 3, new RS at 1 (surge)
kubectl describe pod -n drill -l app=frontend | grep -A3 FailedScheduling   # Insufficient cpu on the surge pod

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
# undo back to the known-good revision rather than fighting the stuck rollout:
kubectl rollout undo deployment/frontend -n drill
kubectl rollout status deployment/frontend -n drill                 # converges cleanly back to 3/3

commands.label: Cleanup
commands.code: kubectl delete namespace drill

problems.title: 'kubectl rollout undo' rolls straight into the SAME broken state
problems.symptom: The 'gateway' deployment in drill just broke after a deploy. On-call runs 'kubectl rollout undo' expecting an instant fix. The pods come back — still broken, in exactly the same way.
problems.hint: 'rollout undo' rolls back to a specific PREVIOUS revision — it assumes that revision was actually healthy. Check what that revision's history actually looked like before trusting it blindly.
problems.diagnosis: rollout undo runs successfully, no error. get pods -> new pods come up, but CrashLoopBackOff persists, same symptom as before the undo. rollout history deployment/gateway -n drill -> shows revision 3 (current, broken) and revision 2 — checking revision 2's actual image with 'rollout history --revision=2' shows it ALSO references the broken config; the last genuinely-working state was revision 1, two steps back, not one.
problems.rootCause: 'kubectl rollout undo' with no --to-revision flag rolls back exactly ONE step, to the immediately prior revision — it has no concept of 'the last revision that was actually healthy,' only 'the previous one in history.' Here, revision 2 was ALSO broken (a bad config change that shipped two deploys in a row before anyone caught it), so a single undo just replays the same failure from one revision back, giving the appearance that rollback 'didn't work' when it actually worked exactly as designed — it just wasn't pointed at a healthy target.
problems.fix: Check 'kubectl rollout history' and inspect each candidate revision's actual image/config with '--revision=N' before undoing, then target the specific known-good revision explicitly with 'kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=N' rather than trusting a bare undo after multiple bad deploys in a row.
problems.mental: Never treat 'rollout undo' as an unconditional safety net — it's a pointer move to a specific numbered revision, not a search for 'the last time this worked.' After ANY incident involving more than one recent deploy, check history and inspect the target revision explicitly before undoing; a bare undo is only reliably safe when you're certain exactly one bad deploy happened.

commands.label: Setup (break it, twice in a row)
commands.code:
kubectl create namespace drill
kubectl -n drill create deployment gateway --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1
kubectl rollout status deployment/gateway -n drill --timeout=60s      # revision 1, healthy
kubectl set image -n drill deployment/gateway gateway=nginx:1.27-alpin --record 2>/dev/null; kubectl annotate deployment gateway -n drill kubernetes.io/change-cause='bad tag' --overwrite   # revision 2, broken
kubectl set image -n drill deployment/gateway gateway=nginx:1.27-alpin-v2 --record 2>/dev/null; kubectl annotate deployment gateway -n drill kubernetes.io/change-cause='still broken' --overwrite   # revision 3, also broken

commands.label: Diagnose
commands.code:
kubectl get pods -n drill                                  # ImagePullBackOff / CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl rollout undo deployment/gateway -n drill            # one step back, to revision 2
kubectl get pods -n drill                                   # STILL broken — revision 2 was bad too
kubectl rollout history deployment/gateway -n drill
kubectl rollout history deployment/gateway -n drill --revision=1   # confirm this is the actually-healthy one

commands.label: Fix
commands.code:
kubectl rollout undo deployment/gateway -n drill --to-revision=1
kubectl rollout status deployment/gateway -n drill          # 1/1 Running, genuinely healthy this time
