myNotes.title: RBAC — Role-Based Access Control
myNotes.body:
RBAC — Role-Based Access Control
RBAC stands for Role-Based Access Control. It is the Kubernetes system used to control what a user, ServiceAccount, or other identity is allowed to do in the cluster.
In simple terms:
RBAC = Who can do what, and where?
For example, suppose your api-sa ServiceAccount should be allowed to read Pods but should not be allowed to delete them.
ServiceAccount: api-sa
        ↓
      Role
        ↓
  Permissions
        ↓
get Pods ✅
list Pods ✅
delete Pods ❌

Main RBAC components
Role
 ↓
Defines permissions within a namespace

ClusterRole
 ↓
Defines permissions at cluster level

RoleBinding
 ↓
Connects a Role to a user/ServiceAccount

ClusterRoleBinding
 ↓
Connects a ClusterRole to a user/ServiceAccount

Example:
ServiceAccount
      ↓
RoleBinding
      ↓
Role
      ↓
"Can get/list Pods"

Easy way to remember:
RBAC = Kubernetes security system that decides which identity can perform which actions on which resources.

myNotes.title: ConfigMap
myNotes.body:
A ConfigMap is a Kubernetes object used to store non-sensitive configuration data separately from the application/container image. It allows the same application to use different configurations in different environments without rebuilding the image.
Main purpose
Application Image
       +
   ConfigMap
       ↓
    Container

Example:
data:
  ENV: prod
  LOG_LEVEL: INFO
  PORT: "8080"

So the image can remain the same:
catalog-service:1.4.2

while configuration can change:
DEV     → ENV=dev
STAGING → ENV=staging
PROD    → ENV=prod

-------------------------------------------------------------------

myNotes.title: Ingress
myNotes.body:
Kubernetes Ingress
Ingress is a Kubernetes resource used to control external HTTP/HTTPS traffic coming into the cluster and route it to different Services.
Think of Ingress as a traffic controller at the entrance of your Kubernetes cluster.
Simple example
Suppose you have two applications:
                  Internet
                     ↓
                  Ingress
                /          \
               ↓            ↓
          /api/users      /shop
              ↓              ↓
        user-service     shop-service
              ↓              ↓
            Pods           Pods

Why do we need Ingress?
Without Ingress, you could expose each application separately using Services such as:
LoadBalancer → user-service
LoadBalancer → shop-service
LoadBalancer → payment-service
That can become expensive and difficult to manage.

With Ingress:
                 One entry point
                      ↓
                   Ingress
              ┌───────┼────────┐
              ↓       ↓        ↓
           Service  Service  Service
              ↓       ↓        ↓
             Pods    Pods      Pods

So Ingress provides routing rules through one entry point.
Example Ingress rule

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  rules:
  - host: example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-service
            port:
              number: 80

This basically says:
If someone requests example.com/api, send the request to web-service on port 80.

One important point
Creating an Ingress object doesn't by itself make traffic work. You also need an Ingress Controller, such as NGINX Ingress Controller, to actually process the Ingress rules.
The overall flow is:
Internet
   ↓
Ingress Controller
   ↓
Ingress rules
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Pods
***************************
Understand the rule
The important part is:
drill.example.com/*=web:80

Read it as:
For any path (/*) on drill.example.com, send the request to the web Service on port 80.
For example:
http://drill.example.com/
              ↓
          Ingress
              ↓
         web:80 Service
              ↓
            Pods
And:
http://drill.example.com/login
              ↓
          Ingress
              ↓
         web:80 Service
And:
http://drill.example.com/api
              ↓
          Ingress
              ↓
         web:80 Service

Because /* means all paths.
Think of the traffic flow
User
 ↓
drill.example.com
 ↓
Ingress: web
 ↓
Rule: /* → web:80
 ↓
Service: web
 ↓
Pods

Important point
The Ingress sends traffic to the Service, not directly to the Pods.
So the architecture is:

Ingress
   ↓
Service (web:80)
   ↓
Pods

Easy way to remember
--rule="HOST/PATH=SERVICE:PORT"
For this command:
drill.example.com/*=web:80 = All requests for drill.example.com go to the web Service on port 80.
**********************************
Why do we need IngressClass ?
You might have multiple Ingress Controllers in one cluster:

Cluster
 ├── nginx controller
 ├── traefik controller
 └── another controller
IngressClass helps determine which controller should handle a particular Ingress.
For example:
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx

means:
"Handle this Ingress using the nginx IngressClass/controller."
Important distinction
Ingress:Defines how traffic should be routed.
example.com/api → web-service

IngressClass:Defines which Ingress Controller should process those rules.
Ingress → nginx controller
Ingress Controller:
The actual software that watches Ingress resources and implements the routing.

Easy way to remember
kubectl get ingressclass = Show which Ingress classes/controllers are available in the cluster.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## `kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml`
**Main definition for notes:**
> **This command creates or updates the Kubernetes resources defined in `ingress.yaml` and makes the cluster match the configuration specified in that file.**
kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml

### How it works
Suppose `ingress.yaml` contains:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: drill
spec:
  rules:
  - host: drill.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80

When you run:
kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml

Kubernetes reads the YAML and applies it to the cluster:
ingress.yaml
     ↓
kubectl apply
     ↓
Kubernetes API Server
     ↓
Ingress: web
     ↓
web Service
     ↓
Pods
### If Ingress doesn't exist
Kubernetes **creates it**.
YAML → Ingress doesn't exist → CREATE

### If Ingress already exists
Kubernetes **updates it** according to the YAML.

YAML → Ingress already exists → UPDATE
For example, if the existing Ingress has:
host: old.example.com
and you change the file to:

host: drill.example.com

then:
kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml

updates the Ingress configuration.
### Why use `-f`?
`-f` means:
> **Read the Kubernetes configuration from this file.**
So:
-f ingress.yaml
means Kubernetes should use `ingress.yaml` as the configuration.

myNotes.title: Difference
myNotes.body:
diff vs apply  
kubectl diff:  "What will change if I apply this file?"  
kubectl apply:  "Apply these changes to the cluster."  
Easy way to remember  
diff = preview changes 
apply = apply changes
-------------------------------
kubectl replace:
Replace the existing resource with the complete configuration from the file.
kubectl apply:
Apply the changes from the file and update the resource toward the desired state.
-------------------------------
Ingress vs Service
This distinction is important:
Service:Provides a stable way to reach Pods.
Service → Pods
Ingress:Provides HTTP/HTTPS routing to Services.
Ingress → Service → Pods
---------------------------------------------------------------
Compare with your previous command
kubectl get pods -n drill -l app=web,env=prod
means:
app=web AND env=prod
While:

kubectl get pods -n drill -l 'app in (web,api)'
means:
app=web OR app=api
Easy way to remember:
in = match any value from the list.

-----------------------------------------------------
Label vs Annotation
This is important:
LABEL
 ↓
Used to identify/select resources
 ↓
kubectl get pods -l app=web
ANNOTATION
 ↓
Stores extra metadata/information
 ↓
Notes, configuration, tool information, etc.
So env=prod would typically be a label, while note=checked-by-abhi is suitable as an annotation.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Both are Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler events that tell you whether a pending Pod caused the cluster to consider adding a node.
NotTriggerScaleUp means the pending Pod did not trigger a node scale-up. The Cluster Autoscaler checked the available node groups and determined that adding a node would not make the Pod schedulable—for example, the Pod's resource requirements, node selector, taint/toleration, affinity, or other constraints may not match any node group.

TriggeredScaleUp means the pending Pod did trigger a cluster scale-up. The Cluster Autoscaler determined that adding a node from a suitable node group could allow the Pod to be scheduled, so it requested additional capacity.

Easy way to remember:
NotTriggerScaleUp → "Adding a node won't solve this Pod's problem."
TriggeredScaleUp → "Adding a node can solve this, so scale the cluster up."

myNotes.title: Label Vs Selector
myNotes.body:
What is a label in Kubernetes?
Answer: A label is a key-value pair attached to a Kubernetes object such as a Pod, Deployment, or Service.
Example:
labels:
  app: web
Here:
Key = app
Value = web

What is a label selector?
A selector, on the other hand, is used to find or filter resources based on their labels. For example, -l app=web is a selector that tells Kubernetes to find Pods whose label is app=web. In simple terms, a label is like a tag attached to an object, while a selector is like a filter used to find objects having that tag. So, app=web on a Pod is the label, while -l app=web in kubectl get pods -l app=web is the selector.


Which Kubernetes resources can have labels?
Answer:
Almost every Kubernetes resource can have labels, including:
Pods
Deployments
Services
ReplicaSets
StatefulSets
DaemonSets
Nodes
Namespaces
Jobs
ConfigMaps
Secrets

What happens when you use -l app=web?
Answer: Kubernetes filters the Pods and returns only Pods having app=web.
For example:
Pod 1 → app=web       ✅
Pod 2 → app=api       ❌
Pod 3 → app=web       ✅
Result:
Pod 1
Pod 3


Can a Pod have multiple labels?
Answer: Yes.
Example:
labels:
  app: web
  environment: production
  version: v2
The Pod has three labels:
app=web
environment=production
version=v2


Can we select using multiple labels?
Answer: Yes.
Example:
kubectl get pods -n drill -l app=web,environment=production
This means:
Find Pods where app=web AND environment=production.

myNotes.title: GKE Q&A
myNotes.body:
what's the smallest unit in Kubernetes?":
"The container is the smallest unit of execution, but the Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules and manages. You never scale, restart, or schedule a container on its own — only a Pod."

Node "Standard vs Autopilot — when would you pick each?
Standard = you manage nodes, Google manages the control plane.
Autopilot = Google manages nodes and control plane; you only manage workloads (pods).

what's the relationship between gcloud and kubectl?":
"gcloud manages the cluster as infrastructure — creating, resizing, upgrading, deleting it. kubectl manages workloads running inside an existing cluster. get-credentials is the bridge: it authenticates kubectl to talk to a cluster gcloud already provisioned, but it doesn't give kubectl any of gcloud's infrastructure-level abilities."

"how does kubectl connect to GKE?":
"kubectl itself is cloud-agnostic — it just talks to whatever Kubernetes API server is listed as the current context in ~/.kube/config. gcloud container clusters get-credentials is the GCP-specific step that populates that file with GKE's API server address and wires up an auth plugin that fetches fresh tokens from your gcloud identity. From there, every request is gated by GCP IAM first, then Kubernetes RBAC."

why multiple node pools?":
"To match hardware to workload — different machine types, sizes, or pricing models (spot vs on-demand) — and scale each independently, with taints/node-selectors controlling which pods are allowed to schedule onto which pool."

note
One cluster → contains multiple node pools → each pool is a group of identical nodes (same machine type/size) → each pool's node count can be scaled independently of the others.
A cluster doesn't have to have all its nodes be the same size or type. Instead, GKE lets you group nodes into pools — and every node inside one pool is identical (same machine type, same disk size, same settings). If you want two different kinds of machines (say, cheap small ones for regular apps and expensive GPU ones for ML), you create two separate pools, each with its own name.

refEdits.kubectl::kubectl config set-context --cu:
The two ways to scope a namespace — and when to use each

Per-command, explicit (-n) — you type it every time:

bash
kubectl get pods -n drill
kubectl logs web-abc123 -n drill
kubectl delete pod web-abc123 -n drill

Pro: always visible, always obvious which namespace you're touching — safer when you're juggling multiple namespaces (like a real staging vs prod split), since you can't accidentally forget which one you're in.
Con: more typing, easy to forget.

Context default (set-context --current --namespace=) — set once, applies everywhere:

bash
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=drill
kubectl get pods            # no -n needed anymore, defaults to drill

Pro: faster for focused solo practice sessions like yours.
Con: the exact risk we flagged earlier — you can forget it's set and accidentally act on drill when you meant somewhere else.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl cordon gk3-terraform-gk:
Why you'd cordon manually?
it's step one of safely taking a node offline — for example, before a manual maintenance window, or before removing a node from a pool. Cordoning first means new workloads stop landing there, so when you're ready to actually empty it out, you're not fighting the scheduler trying to place new pods on a node you're about to shut down.

The three-command maintenance sequence, in order (this ties directly to the pattern in your reference tab):

kubectl cordon <node> — stop new pods from scheduling here.
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets — evict the pods already running here (they get rescheduled onto other nodes). This is the step that actually moves workloads off.
kubectl uncordon <node> — once maintenance is done and the node's back, make it schedulable again.
Important distinction to remember: cordon alone does not move any pods — it only blocks future scheduling. If you cordon a node and stop there, its existing pods just sit there running, unaffected. You need drain specifically to actually evict them. This is a common interview trip-up — people think cordon empties a node; it doesn't, drain does.

Interview-grade one-liner:

"Cordon stops new pods from being scheduled on a node but doesn't touch existing ones — it's the safety step before a drain, which is what actually evicts running pods for maintenance."

Want to keep going through more reference commands like this, or pick back up on drills — I still owe you the "Kubernetes Fundamentals" concept topic we discussed adding to the vault?
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl drain gk3-terraform-gke:
Why --ignore-daemonsets exists

A DaemonSet is a special kind of workload designed to run exactly one pod per node, on every node, permanently — think logging agents, monitoring agents (like Prometheus node-exporter), or CNI networking pods. These aren't meant to be "rescheduled elsewhere" the way a normal Deployment's pods are — their entire purpose is being tied to that specific node.

Because of that, drain refuses to run by default if it finds any DaemonSet-managed pods on the node — it doesn't know what to do with them (they can't be "moved" to another node in the normal sense; moving means running on the new node too, which they might already be doing).

--ignore-daemonsets tells drain: "don't fail because of DaemonSet pods — just leave them running here and drain everything else." This is standard, expected, almost always what you want — that's why it appeared alongside drain in your Command Reference from the start, not as an edge case.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl taint nodes gk3-terrafo:
The one true "anywhere" case

The only way a pod can genuinely go anywhere, ignoring all taints, is if it has a wildcard toleration — one that says "I tolerate everything," which is rare and deliberately used only for special system-level pods (like the ones GKE itself runs for networking/logging). A normal application pod would never be given this.

Full precise version, now that both halves are clear:

A taint blocks everyone except pods with the matching toleration for that specific taint. A toleration only cancels out the one taint it names — it says nothing about other taints elsewhere.

Interview-grade one-liner:

"Tolerations are matched pairwise to taints — a toleration doesn't grant a pod general access, it only neutralizes one specific taint (matching key, value, and effect). A pod could tolerate a GPU taint and still be blocked by a completely different taint on another node."

Node gk3-...-hxq2 has NO taint
→ it's back to being a normal, open node — any pod can schedule there again

refEdits.kubectl::kubectl logs web-595587cc7f-8ln:
-c sidecar
here -c means container.

-c sidecar means:
Show logs from the container named sidecar.
Without -c, if the Pod contains multiple containers, Kubernetes may ask you to specify which container you mean.

show me the logs generated by the sidecar container inside the web-595587cc7f-8ln77 Pod in the drill namespace.

With -f:

Kubernetes keeps the command running and displays new log lines in real time.

What does --previous actually mean?

Old container
     ↓
   CRASHED
     ↓
Kubernetes restarts it
     ↓
New container
     ↓
   RUNNING
Now:

kubectl logs web-595587cc7f-8ln77 -n drill
shows the current/new container's logs.
But:
kubectl logs web-595587cc7f-8ln77 -n drill --previous
shows the logs from the old container that crashed/restarted
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl exec -it web-595587cc7f:
exec = execute command inside container
-it = Give me an interactive terminal
-i means interactive.
It keeps your input connected to the container.
Without -i, you wouldn't have a proper interactive session.
-t means allocate a terminal (TTY).
This makes the shell behave like a normal terminal.

-- = command starts here Everything after this belongs to the command I want to execute inside the container.
/bin/sh = open shell

kubectl exec web-595587cc7f-8ln77 -n drill -- ls
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl exec web-595587cc7f-8ln:
env = Linux command used to display environment variables inside the container.
Show me all environment variables currently available to this process/container.
So you're not opening a shell.
You're directly executing the Linux env command inside the container
For example, you might get:
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
HOSTNAME=web-595587cc7f-8ln77
APP_ENV=production
DB_HOST=mysql-service
DB_PORT=3306
LOG_LEVEL=INFO
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl debug web-595587cc7f-8l:
--image=busybox tells Kubernetes:
Use the BusyBox container image for the debugging environment.
BusyBox is a very small Linux image containing many basic utilities.

Once inside, you might be able to use:
ls
ps
cat
wget
nslookup
ip

exec vs debug

kubectl exec
kubectl exec -it POD -n NAMESPACE -- /bin/sh
Means:Enter/use the existing container.
Pod
│
└── Existing container
       ↑
       │
     exec

kubectl debug
kubectl debug POD -n NAMESPACE -it --image=busybox
Means:Create/use a debugging environment to investigate the Pod.

Conceptually:
Pod
│
├── Application container
│
└── Temporary debug container
          ↑
          │
        debug


kubectl logs
    ↓
"What is the application saying?"

kubectl exec
    ↓
"Let me enter the existing container."

kubectl debug
    ↓
"Give me a debugging environment to investigate the Pod."
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete pod web-595587cc:
this will Delete a specific Pod.

If the Pod is managed by a Deployment/ReplicaSet:
Pod deleted → Controller notices → Replacement Pod created.
This is a practical demonstration of Kubernetes' self-healing / desired-state mechanism.

Note: 
If you created the Pod directly:
kubectl run web ...
and delete it, Kubernetes may not recreate it, because there may be no Deployment/ReplicaSet managing it.

But if it's managed by a Deployment:
Deployment
    ↓
ReplicaSet
    ↓
  Pod
the controller maintains the desired number of Pods

You can copy a local file into a Pod:
kubectl cp ./nginx.conf drill/web-595587cc7f-8ln77:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf

Pod → Local

refEdits.kubectl::kubectl port-forward pod/web-59:
Why use port-forward?
It's especially useful for testing and debugging.

For example, your application is running inside Kubernetes but doesn't have an externally accessible Service.
Instead of exposing it publicly, you can temporarily do:

kubectl port-forward pod/web-595587cc7f-8ln77 8080:80 -n drill
Then test it locally.
Important: it's temporary

The port-forward stays active only while the command is running.
If you press:Ctrl + C the forwarding stops.
Your Pod is not deleted.

8080 = your local machine's port
80 = Pod's port
8080:80 = Local → Pod
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create deployment web -:
Create a Kubernetes Deployment named web in the drill namespace, using the nginx:alpine image.
A Deployment manages your application's Pods.
The relationship is:
Deployment
    ↓
ReplicaSet
    ↓
   Pod
    ↓
Container
    ↓
nginx:alpine

So when you run:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:alpine -n drill
Kubernetes roughly creates:

Deployment: web
       ↓
ReplicaSet: web-xxxxxxxxxx
       ↓
Pod: web-xxxxxxxxxx-xxxxx
       ↓
Container: nginx:alpine
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl scale deployment web --: It changes the desired replica count of the web Deployment in the drill namespace to 5. Kubernetes then creates or removes Pods as necessary so that 5 replicas are running.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl set image deployment/we:
In the web Deployment, change the image of the container named web to nginx:1.27-alpine.
kubectl	Kubernetes command-line tool
set image	Change the container image
deployment/web	Target the web Deployment
web=	Name of the container inside the Deployment
nginx:1.27-alpine	New container image and tag
-n drill	Use the drill namespace

Deployment: web
Container:
web → nginx:1.26

Kubernetes changes:
nginx:1.26
      ↓
nginx:1.27-alpine
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl rollout status deployme:
This command is used to check the progress of a Deployment rollout.

It monitors the rollout of the web Deployment in the drill namespace and shows whether the updated Pods have been successfully created and become ready. It is commonly used after changing the Deployment, such as with kubectl set image, to verify that the rolling update completed successfully.

These commands do different things:
kubectl set image ...
👉 Starts the change

kubectl rollout status ...
👉 Checks whether the change is progressing successfully

kubectl rollout history ...
👉 Shows previous Deployment revisions

kubectl rollout undo ...
👉 Rolls back to a previous revision
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl rollout history deploym:
This command is used to view the rollout history and previous revisions of a Deployment.
What is a revision?

Every time you make a change to the Deployment's Pod template, Kubernetes can create a new revision.

For example:

Revision 1 → nginx:1.26
Revision 2 → nginx:1.27
Revision 3 → nginx:1.27-alpine
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl rollout undo deployment:
Suppose you updated your application:

Revision 1 → nginx:1.26
Revision 2 → nginx:1.27
Revision 3 → nginx:1.27-alpine  ❌

If the latest version has a problem, run:

kubectl rollout undo deployment/web -n drill

Kubernetes rolls the Deployment back:

nginx:1.27-alpine
        ↓
    ROLLBACK
        ↓
nginx:1.27

Kubernetes then performs a rolling update to replace the current Pods with Pods using the previous revision.

This command is used to roll back the web Deployment to a specific previous revision, in this case Revision 2.

undo = go back
--to-revision=2 = go back specifically to revision 2
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl rollout pause deploymen: kubectl rollout pause temporarily pauses a Deployment's rollout, allowing multiple changes to be made before resuming the rollout with kubectl rollout resume.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl rollout restart deploym:
This command is used to restart all Pods of a Deployment by triggering a new rollout, without changing the Deployment's image or configuration
A rollout restart can be useful when:

An application inside the Pods is behaving unexpectedly.
You want to refresh Pods without changing the application version.
Pods need to pick up certain changes that are applied through their startup process.
You want to force a fresh Pod rollout.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl edit deployment web -n: This command opens the web Deployment configuration in an editor so you can directly modify its Kubernetes YAML configuration.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl diff -f deployment.yaml: This command shows the differences between the Kubernetes resource currently running in the cluster and the configuration defined in deployment.yaml, without applying the changes.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl patch deployment web -n:
kubectl patch = make a targeted change to an existing Kubernetes resource without editing the entire YAML.
And in this specific command:
/spec/replicas is changed to 4.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl replace -f deployment.y:
kubectl replace -f deployment.yaml → Replaces an existing Kubernetes resource with the configuration in the YAML file. The resource must already exist.

And:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml → Creates the resource if needed or updates the existing resource toward the configuration defined in the YAML.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete deployment web -: This command deletes the web Deployment from the drill namespace, along with the Pods managed by that Deployment.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get rs -n drill:
kubectl get rs = Show ReplicaSets and their Pod status.
A ReplicaSet (RS) is a Kubernetes resource that makes sure the required number of identical Pods are running.
Deployment: web
      ↓
ReplicaSet: web-7d8f9c
      ↓
Pod
Pod
Pod

If the Deployment says:
replicas: 3
the ReplicaSet tries to keep 3 Pods running.

Example output
NAME               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
web-7d8f9c6d8      3         3         3       10m
web-5f6d7c8b9      0         0         0       20m

Meaning:
DESIRED → How many Pods the ReplicaSet wants.
CURRENT → How many Pods currently exist.
READY → How many Pods are ready to serve traffic.
AGE → How long the ReplicaSet has existed.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl autoscale deployment we: This command creates a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for the web Deployment that automatically adjusts the number of Pods between 2 and 10 based on CPU utilization, targeting 70% CPU usage.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get hpa -n drill:
This command is used to view the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) resources and their current scaling status in the drill namespace.
HPA automatically increases or decreases the number of Pods based on resource usage, such as CPU or memory.

For example, you previously created one with:
kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70 -n drill
That creates an HPA for the web Deployment.
You can then check it with:
kubectl get hpa -n drill
Example output:
NAME   REFERENCE          TARGETS   MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS   AGE
web    Deployment/web     45%/70%   2         10        3          5m
Understand the output
45%/70%
means:
Current CPU = 45%
Target CPU  = 70%
And:
MINPODS = 2
MAXPODS = 10
REPLICAS = 3
means Kubernetes is currently running 3 Pods, and HPA can adjust that number between 2 and 10.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe hpa web -n dri:
get hpa = Quick HPA status
describe hpa = Detailed HPA information and troubleshooting detail
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete hpa web -n drill:
kubectl delete hpa = Remove automatic Pod scaling, but don't delete the Deployment itself.

Deleting the HPA does not delete the Deployment or its Pods.

For example, if the Deployment currently has 5 Pods:

Deployment web
 ↓
Pod 1
Pod 2
Pod 3
Pod 4
Pod 5

Deleting the HPA does not immediately delete those 5 Pods.

It simply means:

Kubernetes will no longer use that HPA to automatically increase or decrease the replica count.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl expose deployment web -:
This command creates a Kubernetes Service for the web Deployment, exposing port 80 on the Service and forwarding traffic to port 8080 on the Pods.

Client
  |
  | Port 80
  ↓
Service
  |
  | forwards to port 8080
  ↓
Pod
  |
  | Port 8080
  ↓
Application
Service port  = 80
Pod port      = 8080

For example, 
when a client sends:
Service:80
the Service forwards the traffic to:
Pod:8080

What Service gets created?

The command creates a Service, typically named after the Deployment:
web
You can verify it:
kubectl get svc -n drill
Example:
NAME   TYPE       CLUSTER-IP      PORT(S)
web    ClusterIP  10.96.100.10    80/TCP
Important point
kubectl expose creates a Service. It does not create another Deployment or another set of Pods.

Create a Service on port 80 and send that traffic to port 8080 of the web Pods."
Easy way to remember
--port = Service port
--target-port = Pod/application port
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create service clusteri:
This command creates a ClusterIP Service named web in the drill namespace that exposes Service port 80 and forwards TCP traffic to port 8080.
Service type = ClusterIP
Service port 80 → target port 8080

What is ClusterIP?
ClusterIP is the default Kubernetes Service type.
It provides a stable internal IP that can be accessed from inside the Kubernetes cluster.
Inside cluster
      |
      ↓
ClusterIP Service
web:80
      |
      ↓
Pods:8080
It is normally not directly accessible from the public internet.

Important difference from kubectl expose
Earlier you had:
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=8080 -n drill
That command:
Creates a Service based on the web Deployment.
Here:
kubectl create service clusterip web --tcp=80:8080 -n drill
you are explicitly creating a ClusterIP Service.
⚠️ Important practical point
kubectl create service clusterip does not automatically know that this Service should select the Pods belonging to your web Deployment just because the Service is also named web.
A Service needs a selector to know which Pods to send traffic to.

For example:

selector:
  app: web

If the Service has no matching selector, you can have:

Client
  ↓
Service
  ↓
❌ No matching Pods
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get svc -n drill: This command is used to list all Services in the drill namespace and see their basic information.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe svc web -n dri: This command shows detailed information about the web Service in the drill namespace, including its type, IP address, ports, selectors, endpoints, and events
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get endpoints web -n dr:
This command shows the actual Pod IP addresses and ports that the web Service is currently sending traffic to.
What are Endpoints?
A Service provides a stable way to access Pods, but Pods can come and go and their IP addresses can change.
Endpoints tell the Service where the currently matching Pods are located.

Think:
Service: web
      ↓
   Endpoints
      ↓
┌─────┼─────┐
↓     ↓     ↓
Pod1  Pod2  Pod3
IP    IP    IP
Example output
NAME   ENDPOINTS                                  AGE
web    10.244.0.5:8080,10.244.0.6:8080           10m
This means the web Service currently has two endpoints:
10.244.0.5:8080
10.244.0.6:8080

Traffic can be forwarded to these Pod IP/port combinations.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get endpointslices -l k:
get	Display Kubernetes resources
endpointslices	Show EndpointSlice resources
-l	Filter resources using a label selector "Only show EndpointSlices whose label says they belong to the web Service."
kubernetes.io/service-name=web	Select EndpointSlices belonging to the web Service
-n drill	Look inside the drill namespace

What is EndpointSlice?
An EndpointSlice stores information about the network endpoints behind a Service.
In simple terms:
Service
   ↓
EndpointSlice
   ↓
Pod IP + Port

For example:
Service: web
     ↓
EndpointSlice
     ↓
10.244.0.5:8080
10.244.0.6:8080
10.244.0.7:8080
These are the actual endpoints where the Service can send traffic.

Why use EndpointSlices instead of Endpoints?
Both are related, but EndpointSlice is the newer, scalable Kubernetes mechanism for tracking Service endpoints.
The basic idea:
Old:
Service → Endpoints → many Pods
Modern:
Service → EndpointSlices → Pods
EndpointSlices can split a large number of endpoints across multiple objects instead of putting everything into one large Endpoints object.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl port-forward svc/web 80:
`kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 -n drill` is used to **temporarily access the `web` Service from your local computer** without exposing the Service publicly. Here, `8080:80` means **local port 8080 → Service port 80**. For example, if your `web` Service is running inside Kubernetes on port `80`, you run this command and then open `http://localhost:8080` in your browser. Kubernetes forwards your local request from `localhost:8080` to the `web` Service on port `80`, and the Service then sends the request to one of its backend Pods. The port-forward exists only while the command is running; stopping the command removes the connection.
```text
Your Computer
localhost:8080
      ↓
kubectl port-forward
      ↓
Service web:80
      ↓
Pod:8080
```
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete svc web -n drill:
`kubectl delete svc web -n drill` is used to **delete the `web` Service from the `drill` namespace**. It removes the stable network endpoint that was allowing traffic to reach the `web` Pods, but it **does not delete the Deployment or the Pods themselves**. For example, if you have `web` Service → `web` Pods, after running this command the Service is removed, but the Pods continue running normally; they simply no longer have that Service available to receive traffic through its ClusterIP.

```text
Before:
Client
  ↓
Service web
  ↓
Pods

After deleting Service:

Service web ❌
      ↓
Pods ✅ still running
```
**Easy way to remember:** `delete svc` = **remove the Service, not the Pods or Deployment.**
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete all --all -n dri:
`kubectl delete all --all -n drill` is used to **delete all resources covered by the `all` resource group in the `drill` namespace**. The first `all` means the resource group, while the second `--all` means **all objects of those resource types**, not just one named resource. For example, it can remove resources such as **Pods, Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Services** from the `drill` namespace. It does **not mean absolutely every Kubernetes resource type** in the namespace; resources such as ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, and some other resource types are not included simply because you used `all`.

kubectl delete all --all -n drill

        ↓

drill namespace
        ↓
┌──────────────────────┐
│ Pods          ❌      │
│ Deployments   ❌      │
│ ReplicaSets   ❌      │
│ Services      ❌      │
└──────────────────────┘
Other resources may still exist
(ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, etc.)
**Easy way to remember:**
> **`delete all --all` = Delete all common workload/network resources selected by `all` in that namespace.**
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get ingress -n drill:
kubectl get ingress -n drill is used to list all Ingress resources in the drill namespace and see their basic information. An Ingress manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to services inside a Kubernetes cluster, usually based on a hostname or URL path. For example, if you have an Ingress that routes example.com/api to the web Service, this command lets you check whether that Ingress exists and see its configured hosts and addres

Example output:

NAME    CLASS   HOSTS          ADDRESS       PORTS   AGE
web     nginx   example.com    10.0.0.100    80      5m

Here, web is the Ingress name, nginx is the Ingress class/controller, example.com is the hostname being handled, 10.0.0.100 is the address through which traffic can reach the Ingress, and 80 indicates HTTP traffic.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create ingress web --ru: This command creates an Ingress named web that routes HTTP requests for the hostname drill.example.com to the web Service on port 80 in the drill namespace.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get ingressclass:
This command lists all IngressClass resources available in the Kubernetes cluster. An IngressClass tells Kubernetes which Ingress Controller should handle an Ingress.
kubectl get ingressclass

Example output:
NAME    CONTROLLER                      PARAMETERS   AGE
nginx   k8s.io/ingress-nginx            <none>       10m

What is IngressClass?
Think of it like this:

Ingress
   ↓
IngressClass
   ↓
Ingress Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Pods

For example, if you have:
IngressClass: nginx
Controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
it means an NGINX Ingress Controller is responsible for processing Ingress resources that use that class.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe ingress web -n:
This command shows detailed information about the web Ingress in the drill namespace, including its rules, host, paths, backend Service, IngressClass, address, and events.

kubectl describe ingress web -n drill
Example You might see:

Name:             web
Namespace:        drill
Address:          10.0.0.100
Ingress Class:    nginx
Rules:
  Host                Path  Backends
  ----                ----  --------
  drill.example.com   /     web:80
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml: This command creates or updates the Kubernetes resources defined in ingress.yaml and makes the cluster match the configuration specified in that file.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete ingress web -n d:
This command deletes the web Ingress resource from the drill namespace, removing the Ingress routing rules that direct external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the web Service

For example, suppose you have:
Internet
   ↓
Ingress: web
   ↓
web Service :80
   ↓
Pods

After running:kubectl delete ingress web -n drill

the Ingress is removed:
Internet
   ↓
Ingress ❌
   
web Service :80
   ↓
Pods ✅

The web Service and its Pods are not deleted. Only the Ingress and its routing configuration are removed. Therefore, traffic that depended on that Ingress hostname/path will no longer be routed through that Ingress.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create configmap app-co:
This command creates a ConfigMap named app-config in the drill namespace and stores a non-sensitive configuration value ENV=prod inside it.
--from-literal	Create data directly from a key-value pair
ENV=prod	Key = ENV, Value = prod
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create configmap nginx-:
kubectl create configmap nginx-conf --from-file=nginx.conf -n drill is used to create a ConfigMap named nginx-conf and store the contents of the local nginx.conf file inside it. Here, --from-file=nginx.conf tells Kubernetes to read the configuration file from your current directory and put its contents into the ConfigMap, while -n drill specifies that the ConfigMap should be created in the drill namespace. For example, if nginx.conf contains NGINX configuration such as server { listen 80; }, Kubernetes stores that configuration in nginx-conf, which can later be mounted into a Pod as a file so that NGINX can use it.

nginx.conf file
      ↓
kubectl create configmap
      ↓
ConfigMap: nginx-conf
      ↓
Pod mounts ConfigMap
      ↓
NGINX uses nginx.conf

Easy way to remember:
--from-file = Take a configuration file from your computer and store its contents inside a ConfigMap.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get configmap -n drill:
kubectl get configmap -n drill is used to list all ConfigMaps available in the drill namespace and see their basic information. The command does not show the actual configuration values; it mainly shows the ConfigMap names and some metadata such as how much data each ConfigMap contains and how long ago it was created. For example, if you previously created app-config and nginx-conf, running this command may show app-config and nginx-conf in the list. To see the actual contents of a particular ConfigMap, you can use kubectl describe configmap app-config -n drill or kubectl get configmap app-config -n drill -o yaml.

kubectl get configmap -n drill
        ↓
Find all ConfigMaps
        ↓
drill namespace
        ↓
app-config
nginx-conf

Easy way to remember:
get configmap = Check which ConfigMaps exist in the namespace.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get configmap app-confi: kubectl get configmap app-config -n drill -o yaml is used to display the complete app-config ConfigMap in YAML format, including its metadata and the actual configuration data stored inside it. Here, app-config is the ConfigMap name, -n drill specifies the namespace, and -o yaml tells Kubernetes to show the resource in YAML format instead of the normal short table.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create secret generic a:
This command creates a Kubernetes Secret named api-cfg in the drill namespace and stores the value DATABASE_URL=postgres://demo inside it. The --from-literal option means you are providing the secret value directly on the command line instead of reading it from a file. Kubernetes stores Secret data in a base64-encoded representation, but base64 is encoding, not encryption, so Secrets should still be protected with proper Kubernetes security controls. The purpose is to keep sensitive configuration such as database URLs, passwords, API keys, and tokens separate from your application configuration.

DATABASE_URL=postgres://demo
          ↓
   kubectl create secret
          ↓
Secret: api-cfg
          ↓
     drill namespace
          ↓
Pod / Application

generic = create a normal, general-purpose Secret for your own key-value data.

ConfigMap → non-sensitive configuration
Secret → sensitive configuration
generic Secret → general-purpose Secret data such as passwords, tokens, API keys, and database credentials.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create secret docker-re:
This command creates a Kubernetes Docker registry Secret named regcred in the drill namespace. Its purpose is to give Kubernetes the credentials required to authenticate to a private container image registry, in this case asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev, so that Pods can pull private Docker/container images. Here, docker-registry tells Kubernetes that this is a registry-credential Secret, --docker-server specifies the registry address, --docker-username=_json_key specifies the authentication username expected for this Google Artifact Registry JSON-key method, and --docker-password="$(cat key.json)" reads the contents of the local key.json file and supplies it as the password. Kubernetes stores the resulting registry credentials in the Secret, which can later be referenced by a Pod using imagePullSecrets.

Private Registry
      ↓
asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev
      ↑
   Credentials
      ↑
   Secret: regcred
      ↑
   Pod uses imagePullSecrets

For example, a Pod can reference it like:
spec:
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: regcred
Then when Kubernetes needs to pull a private image:

Pod
 ↓
imagePullSecrets: regcred
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Private Registry
 ↓
Container Image

Easy way to remember:
docker-registry Secret = store container-registry login credentials so Kubernetes can pull private images.

Security note: key.json contains a credential, so don't commit it to Git or expose it in logs. Also, Google recommends using more secure authentication mechanisms than long-lived service-account keys where possible
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create secret tls web-t:
This command creates a TLS Secret named web-tls in the drill namespace and stores a TLS certificate and its corresponding private key inside it. The tls part tells Kubernetes that this Secret is specifically for TLS/HTTPS, while --cert=tls.crt provides the certificate file and --key=tls.key provides the matching private key. This Secret is commonly used by an Ingress to enable HTTPS for an application. For example, when a user visits https://drill.example.com, the Ingress can use web-tls to present the TLS certificate and establish an encrypted HTTPS connection.

tls.crt  → TLS Certificate
tls.key  → Private Key
     ↓
Secret: web-tls
     ↓
Ingress
     ↓
HTTPS
     ↓
Service
     ↓
Pods

For example, an Ingress can use it like:

spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - drill.example.com
    secretName: web-tls

Easy way to remember:
kubectl create secret tls = Create a Secret containing a TLS certificate + private key for HTTPS/TLS.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get secrets -n drill:
This command is used to list all Secrets available in the drill namespace and see their basic information. It shows the Secret names, their type, how many data entries they contain, and how long ago they were created. It does not normally display the actual secret values, which helps prevent credentials such as passwords, tokens, and private keys from appearing in the normal output. For example, if you previously created api-cfg, regcred, and web-tls, this command will list those Secrets and their types.

kubectl get secrets -n drill
Example:

NAME       TYPE                             DATA   AGE
api-cfg    Opaque                           1      10m
regcred    kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson   1      8m
web-tls    kubernetes.io/tls                2      5m

Here, api-cfg is a general-purpose Secret, regcred contains container-registry credentials, and web-tls contains a TLS certificate and private key.

Easy way to remember:

kubectl get secrets -n drill = Check which Secrets exist in the drill namespace without displaying their actual values
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get secret api-cfg -n d:
This command is used to **retrieve the `DATABASE_URL` value stored inside the `api-cfg` Secret and decode it from Base64 so you can see the original value**. Kubernetes stores Secret data in Base64-encoded form, so `-o jsonpath='{.data.DATABASE_URL}'` extracts only the `DATABASE_URL` field from the Secret, and `| base64 -d` decodes that value back to its original text. For example, if the Secret contains the encoded value for `postgres://demo`, this command will print `postgres://demo` in the terminal.

Secret: api-cfg
      ↓
.data.DATABASE_URL
      ↓
Base64 encoded value
      ↓
base64 -d
      ↓
Original DATABASE_URL

**Easy way to remember:**
> **`jsonpath` = extract the specific Secret value**
> **`base64 -d` = decode it back to the original value**

⚠️ **Important:** This command exposes the secret directly in your terminal, so don't use it casually in shared terminals, screenshots, logs, or scripts.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl set env deployment/api:
This command is used to set an environment variable named DATABASE_URL in the api Deployment in the drill namespace. The value of that environment variable will be postgres://demo, so containers created by the Deployment can access it as DATABASE_URL. Kubernetes updates the Deployment's Pod template, which normally causes a new rollout, meaning existing Pods are gradually replaced with new Pods containing the updated environment variable.

Deployment: api
      ↓
Set environment variable
      ↓
DATABASE_URL = postgres://demo
      ↓
New Pods
      ↓
Application can read DATABASE_URL
For example, inside the application container:
DATABASE_URL
     ↓
postgres://demo

The command is effectively changing the Deployment configuration from:
api Deployment
    ↓
Old Pod
to:

api Deployment
    ↓
Updated Pod
DATABASE_URL=postgres://demo

Easy way to remember:
kubectl set env deployment/... = Add or change an environment variable in a Deployment's Pods.

⚠️ Important: For real database credentials, don't put passwords directly in the command. Use a Kubernetes Secret and reference the Secret from the Deployment instead.

This command is used to take all key-value pairs from the app-config ConfigMap and add them as environment variables to the api Deployment in the drill namespace. The --from=configmap/app-config tells Kubernetes to read the configuration from the app-config ConfigMap instead of manually specifying each variable. For example, if app-config contains ENV=prod and LOG_LEVEL=INFO, Kubernetes adds both values as environment variables to the Pods created by the api Deployment. Because the Deployment's Pod template is changed, Kubernetes normally starts a new rollout to replace the old Pods with updated Pods.

ConfigMap: app-config
      ↓
ENV=prod
LOG_LEVEL=INFO
      ↓
Deployment: api
      ↓
New Pods
      ↓
Environment variables:
ENV=prod
LOG_LEVEL=INFO

For example, if the ConfigMap contains:
data:
  ENV: prod
  LOG_LEVEL: INFO

the api container can access:
ENV       → prod
LOG_LEVEL → INFO

Easy way to remember:
--from=configmap/app-config = Take the ConfigMap's key-value pairs and make them environment variables in the Deployment's Pods.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete configmap app-co:
This command is used to delete the app-config ConfigMap from the drill namespace. It removes the stored configuration data from Kubernetes, such as ENV=prod, LOG_LEVEL=INFO, etc. It does not directly delete the Deployment or Pods that may be using the ConfigMap. However, what happens to an application after deletion depends on how the Pod was consuming the ConfigMap; for example, existing environment variables already loaded into a running container generally remain until the Pod is recreated, while a mounted ConfigMap can behave differently. If the Deployment later creates a new Pod that expects the deleted ConfigMap, that Pod may fail to start because the required ConfigMap no longer exists.

ConfigMap: app-config
       ↓
       ❌ DELETE
       
Deployment: api
       ↓
Pods → not automatically deleted
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete secret api-cfg -:
This command is used to delete the api-cfg Secret from the drill namespace. Here, kubectl delete secret tells Kubernetes to remove a Secret, api-cfg is the name of the Secret being deleted, and -n drill specifies that the Secret belongs to the drill namespace. For example, if api-cfg contains DATABASE_URL=postgres://demo, running this command removes that Secret from Kubernetes. It does not delete the Deployment or Pods using the Secret. However, if a new Pod is created later and its configuration requires this Secret, the new Pod may fail to start because the Secret no longer exists.

Secret: api-cfg
      ↓
    DELETE
      ↓
Secret removed ❌

Deployment: api
      ↓
Pods continue running ✅

Easy way to remember:
kubectl delete secret = Delete the Secret object and its stored data, not the Pods or Deployment.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get pvc -n drill:
This command is used to list all PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) in the drill namespace and check their current storage status. A PVC is a request from an application/Pod for persistent storage. For example, if a Pod needs 5Gi of storage to save database files or uploaded data, it can use a PVC to request that storage from Kubernetes. The command shows information such as the PVC name, status, the PersistentVolume (PV) it is connected to, requested storage size, and access mode.

kubectl get pvc -n drill

Example output:
NAME          STATUS   VOLUME      CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
app-storage   Bound    pvc-abc123  5Gi        RWO            standard       10m
Here, app-storage is the PVC name, Bound means Kubernetes successfully connected the PVC to a PersistentVolume, pvc-abc123 is the associated PV, 5Gi is the available storage capacity, and RWO means the volume can normally be mounted as read-write by one node at a time.
The basic flow is:
Pod
 ↓
PVC (request for storage)
 ↓
PV (actual storage)
 ↓
Disk / Cloud Storage

Easy way to remember:
kubectl get pvc = Check the storage requests made by applications and whether they are successfully connected to storage.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get pv:
This command is used to list all PersistentVolumes (PVs) available in the Kubernetes cluster and see their storage details. A PersistentVolume (PV) represents the actual storage resource available to Kubernetes, such as a disk, cloud volume, or network storage. Unlike a PVC, a PV is cluster-wide and is not limited to a particular namespace. For example, if a PVC requests 5Gi storage, Kubernetes can bind it to a suitable 5Gi PV.

kubectl get pv
Example output:
NAME        CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM                 STORAGECLASS   AGE
pv-data     5Gi        RWO            Retain           Bound    drill/app-storage     standard       10m
Here, pv-data is the PV name, 5Gi is its storage capacity, RWO means ReadWriteOnce, Retain is the reclaim policy, and Bound means this PV is currently connected to the drill/app-storage PVC.

The relationship is:
Pod
 ↓
PVC  ← storage request
 ↓
PV   ← actual storage
 ↓
Disk / Cloud Storage
PVC vs PV
PVC = "I need 5Gi storage."
PV = "Here is 5Gi storage available to you."

Easy way to remember:
kubectl get pv = Check the actual persistent storage resources available in the entire cluster.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get storageclass:
This command is used to list all StorageClasses available in the Kubernetes cluster. A StorageClass defines how Kubernetes should dynamically create/provision storage when a PVC requests it. In simple terms, the StorageClass acts like a storage template that tells Kubernetes what type of storage to create and which provisioner should create it. For example, if a PVC requests 5Gi using the standard StorageClass, Kubernetes can automatically create a suitable PersistentVolume instead of you manually creating the PV.
Example output:
NAME                 PROVISIONER                     RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE      AGE
standard (default)   kubernetes.io/...              Delete          Immediate              20m

Here, standard is the StorageClass name, (default) means PVCs can use it automatically when no StorageClass is specified, PROVISIONER identifies the component responsible for creating the storage, RECLAIMPOLICY defines what happens to the dynamically created PV when its PVC is deleted, and VOLUMEBINDINGMODE determines when the storage is actually bound to a PVC.

The complete relationship is:
PVC
 │
 │ requests 5Gi
 ↓
StorageClass
 │
 │ dynamically provisions
 ↓
PV
 │
 ↓
Actual Storage

For example:
spec:
  storageClassName: standard
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi

means:
"Give this PVC 5Gi of storage using the standard StorageClass."

Easy way to remember:
StorageClass = blueprint/template that tells Kubernetes how to dynamically create storage for PVCs.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe storageclass s:
This command is used to show detailed information about the standard-rwo StorageClass in the Kubernetes cluster. It helps you understand how Kubernetes dynamically provisions storage when a PVC requests this StorageClass. Unlike PVCs and PVs, StorageClasses are not namespace-specific, so you don't need -n drill.

Name:                 standard-rwo
Provisioner:          pd.csi.storage.gke.io
ReclaimPolicy:        Delete
VolumeBindingMode:    WaitForFirstConsumer
AllowVolumeExpansion: true

Provisioner tells you which storage plugin/driver creates the actual storage. ReclaimPolicy tells Kubernetes what to do with the dynamically created PV when its PVC is deleted; Delete generally means the PV and dynamically provisioned storage are deleted. VolumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer means Kubernetes waits until a Pod actually uses the PVC before selecting/provisioning the storage, which can help choose storage compatible with the Pod's scheduling location. AllowVolumeExpansion: true means the PVC can potentially be increased in size.

The overall flow is:

PVC
 ↓
storageClassName: standard-rwo
 ↓
StorageClass
 ↓
Provisioner
 ↓
PV
 ↓
Actual Storage

Easy way to remember:
describe storageclass = See exactly how a StorageClass provisions and manages storage.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe pvc data-pvc -:
This command is used to show detailed information about the data-pvc PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) in the drill namespace. It helps you understand how much storage the application requested, whether the PVC is successfully connected to a PersistentVolume, which StorageClass is being used, the access mode, and any events explaining storage problems. For example, if data-pvc requests 5Gi and is successfully connected to a PV, you may see Status: Bound, meaning the storage is ready to be used by a Pod
Example:
Name:             data-pvc
Namespace:        drill
Status:           Bound
Volume:           pvc-abc123
StorageClass:     standard-rwo
Access Modes:     RWO
Capacity:         5Gi
VolumeMode:       Filesystem

Here, Status: Bound means the PVC has successfully been connected to a PV, Volume shows the PV associated with the PVC, StorageClass shows which storage provisioning template was used, Access Modes shows how the volume can be mounted, and Capacity shows the storage capacity available.

The bottom of the output contains Events, which are especially useful for troubleshooting. For example, if the PVC is stuck in Pending, the events may tell you whether Kubernetes couldn't find or dynamically provision suitable storage.

PVC: data-pvc
      ↓
StorageClass
      ↓
PV
      ↓
Actual Storage
      ↓
Pod

Easy way to remember:
describe pvc = Get detailed information about a storage request, its bound PV, configuration, and storage-related problems
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml:
This command is used to create or update a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) using the configuration written in pvc.yaml. The -f pvc.yaml tells Kubernetes to read the desired storage configuration from that file, while apply means Kubernetes will create the PVC if it doesn't exist or update it if it already exists. For example, if pvc.yaml requests 5Gi of storage using the standard-rwo StorageClass, Kubernetes creates the PVC and attempts to bind it to a suitable PersistentVolume (or dynamically provision one through the StorageClass). The PVC itself is the request for storage, not the actual storag

pvc.yaml
   ↓
kubectl apply
   ↓
PVC: data-pvc
   ↓
StorageClass
   ↓
PV
   ↓
Actual Storage

Example pvc.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-pvc
  namespace: drill
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
  storageClassName: standard-rwo

If you see:
NAME       STATUS   VOLUME       CAPACITY
data-pvc   Bound    pvc-abc123   5Gi

it means the storage request has successfully been connected to a PV.
Easy way to remember:
kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml = Create/update the PVC according to the storage configuration written in pvc.yaml.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete pvc data-pvc -n:
This command is used to delete the data-pvc PersistentVolumeClaim from the drill namespace. A PVC is the application's request for persistent storage, so deleting it removes that storage request. What happens to the associated PV and underlying storage depends on the PV's Reclaim Policy, such as Delete or Retain. For example, if data-pvc is bound to a PV with Delete reclaim policy, deleting the PVC may cause the dynamically provisioned PV and underlying storage to be deleted as well.

PVC: data-pvc
     ↓
    DELETE ❌
     ↓
PV: pvc-3f8a9c21...
     ↓
Reclaim Policy decides what happens

Easy way to remember:
delete pvc = Delete the application's storage request; the PV/storage may also be affected depending on its reclaim policy.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete pv pvc-3f8a9c21-:
This command is used to delete the specific PersistentVolume (PV) directly from the Kubernetes cluster. Unlike a PVC, a PV represents the actual storage resource registered with Kubernetes. Here, pvc-3f8a9c21-b5d4-4e7a-9c1a-2f6e8d4b1a90 is the name of the PV being deleted. Deleting the PV does not automatically mean the underlying disk/data is deleted; what happens to the actual storage depends on how that PV was provisioned and its reclaim policy.

PV: pvc-3f8a9c21...
       ↓
     DELETE ❌
       ↓
PV object removed from Kubernetes
Main difference
PVC = Application's request for storage
PV  = Storage resource provided to Kubernetes
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete namespace drill:
This command is used to delete the entire drill namespace from the Kubernetes cluster. A Namespace is like a container/group for Kubernetes resources, so when you delete the namespace, Kubernetes also deletes the resources inside that namespace, such as Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, Ingresses, and other namespaced resources. For example, if drill contains web Deployment, web Service, app-config ConfigMap, and api-cfg Secret, deleting the namespace removes those resources along with the namespace itself.

The flow is:
Namespace: drill
      ↓
    DELETE ❌
      ↓
┌─────────────────────┐
│ Deployments   ❌    │
│ Pods          ❌    │
│ Services      ❌    │
│ ConfigMaps    ❌    │
│ Secrets       ❌    │
│ Ingress       ❌    │
│ PVCs          ❌    │
└─────────────────────┘

Important: A namespace deletion is a major cleanup operation. It can remove many resources at once, so you should use it carefully.
Easy way to remember:
kubectl delete namespace drill = Delete the drill namespace and the namespaced resources contained inside it.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl create pdb web-pdb --se:
This command creates a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) named web-pdb in the drill namespace. A PDB is used to protect an application's availability during voluntary disruptions, such as node maintenance, draining a node, or other planned operations that intentionally remove Pods. Here, --selector=app=web tells Kubernetes that the PDB applies to Pods having the label app=web, while --min-available=2 means Kubernetes should try to ensure that at least 2 matching Pods remain available during a voluntary disruption. For example, if you have 5 web Pods, Kubernetes can voluntarily disrupt some of them, but it should not allow the disruption to take the available matching Pods below 2.

web Pods
  ↓
app=web
  ↓
PDB: web-pdb
  ↓
min-available = 2
  ↓
Keep at least 2 available

For example:
5 Pods
 ↓
Node maintenance
 ↓
Some Pods can be disrupted
 ↓
At least 2 should remain available

Important: PDB mainly protects against voluntary disruptions. It does not guarantee that 2 Pods will remain available if Pods fail because of crashes, hardware failure, or other involuntary disruptions.

Easy way to remember:
PDB = "During planned disruption, don't voluntarily take too many of my application's Pods down at once."
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get pdb -n drill:
This command is used to list all PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) in the drill namespace and see their current availability protection. It gives you a quick view of which applications have a PDB configured and whether Kubernetes can currently allow voluntary Pod disruptions. For example, if you created web-pdb with --min-available=2, this command lets you check how many Pods are currently available and how many Pods can safely be disrupted.

Example output:
NAME      MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
web-pdb   2               N/A               1                     10m

Here, MIN AVAILABLE means at least 2 Pods should remain available, and ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 1 means Kubernetes can currently voluntarily disrupt 1 Pod while respecting the PDB.

For example:

5 web Pods available
       ↓
PDB requires minimum 2
       ↓
4 can remain → okay
3 can remain → okay
2 can remain → okay
1 can remain → ❌ not allowed

Easy way to remember:
kubectl get pdb = Quickly check your application's Pod disruption protection and how many voluntary disruptions are currently allowed.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe pdb web-pdb -n:
This command is used to see detailed information about the web-pdb (PodDisruptionBudget) in the drill namespace. It shows which Pods the PDB applies to, how many Pods must remain available, how many are currently available, and how many voluntary Pod disruptions are currently allowed. For example, if the PDB was created with --selector=app=web --min-available=2 and there are 5 matching Pods, Kubernetes tries to keep at least 2 available, so up to 3 Pods could potentially be voluntarily disrupted at that moment.

Example:
Name:                 web-pdb
Namespace:            drill
Min available:        2
Selector:             app=web
Current:              5
Desired:              2
Disruptions allowed:  3

The important part is:

Current available = 5
Minimum required  = 2
                     ↓
Allowed disruption = 5 - 2 = 3
So Kubernetes can allow voluntary disruptions while keeping at least 2 matching Pods available.

Easy way to remember:
describe pdb = Detailed view of your Pod availability protection and how much voluntary disruption is currently allowed.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get networkpolicy -n dr:
This command is used to list all NetworkPolicies in the drill namespace and see which network security policies are configured. A NetworkPolicy controls which Pods are allowed to communicate with other Pods or external network endpoints. For example, a policy might allow the frontend Pods to communicate with backend Pods but block other Pods from accessing the backend.
Example output:

NAME             POD-SELECTOR   AGE
allow-web        app=web        10m
allow-backend    app=backend    5m
Here, allow-web and allow-backend are NetworkPolicy names, while POD-SELECTOR shows which Pods each policy applies to.

The basic idea is:
Pod A
  ↓
NetworkPolicy
  ↓
Allowed? ── Yes → Pod B
       └─ No  → ❌ Blocked

Easy way to remember:
kubectl get networkpolicy = Check which network traffic rules are configured for Pods in the namespace.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe networkpolicy:
This command is used to show detailed information about the deny-all NetworkPolicy in the drill namespace. It helps you understand which Pods the policy applies to and what incoming (Ingress) or outgoing (Egress) network traffic is allowed. For example, a common deny-all policy selects all Pods but defines no allowed traffic, effectively blocking network communication covered by that policy.

If the policy is a typical deny-all policy, you may see something like:
Name:         deny-all
Namespace:    drill
PodSelector:  <all pods>
Policy Types: Ingress

or:

Policy Types: Ingress, Egress
The important concept is:

                NetworkPolicy
                     ↓
              Selects Pods
                     ↓
        ┌────────────┴────────────┐
        ↓                         ↓
     Ingress                    Egress
   Incoming traffic          Outgoing traffic
        ↓                         ↓
     Allowed?                  Allowed?

For example, if it is configured as a deny-all ingress policy:
Other Pod
   ↓
   ❌
web Pod

But remember: the exact behavior depends on the policy's podSelector and policyTypes. NetworkPolicies are also enforced by the cluster's network plugin/CNI; simply creating a NetworkPolicy doesn't guarantee enforcement if the networking implementation doesn't support NetworkPolicy.

Easy way to remember:
describe networkpolicy = See exactly which Pods the policy protects and what network traffic it allows or blocks.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl apply -f netpol.yaml:
This command is used to create or update a NetworkPolicy using the configuration written in netpol.yaml. The -f netpol.yaml tells Kubernetes to read the NetworkPolicy definition from that YAML file, while apply means Kubernetes will create the policy if it doesn't exist or update it if it already exists. For example, if netpol.yaml contains a policy that allows only Pods with app=frontend to communicate with Pods having app=backend, applying the file makes that network rule active in the cluster.

netpol.yaml
     ↓
kubectl apply
     ↓
NetworkPolicy
     ↓
Selects Pods
     ↓
Controls allowed traffic
For example:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend
  namespace: drill
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend

This means:
frontend Pod
     ↓
     ✅
backend Pod

other Pod
     ↓
     ❌
backend Pod

Easy way to remember:
kubectl apply -f netpol.yaml = Create or update the NetworkPolicy according to the rules written in netpol.yaml
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete networkpolicy de:
This command is used to delete the deny-all NetworkPolicy from the drill namespace. The deny-all policy may have been restricting network traffic to or from selected Pods, so deleting it removes that particular set of network rules. It does not delete the Pods, Services, or Deployments themselves. After deletion, the affected Pods may become reachable according to any other NetworkPolicies that still apply to them.

For example, before deletion:
Pod
 ↓
deny-all NetworkPolicy
 ↓
Traffic blocked ❌

After deletion:
Pod
 ↓
deny-all ❌ removed
 ↓
Other NetworkPolicies / normal networking rules
Important: Deleting one NetworkPolicy does not automatically mean "allow all traffic." If another NetworkPolicy still selects the same Pods, its rules can continue to restrict traffic.

Easy way to remember:
delete networkpolicy = Remove that specific network traffic policy; it does not delete the Pods or Services.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get daemonset -n drill:
This command is used to list all DaemonSets in the drill namespace and see their basic status. A DaemonSet ensures that a copy of a Pod runs on each eligible node in the Kubernetes cluster. For example, if a DaemonSet is configured to run on all worker nodes and you have 3 eligible nodes, Kubernetes normally creates 3 Pods—one on each node.

Example output:
NAME       DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
log-agent  3         3         3       3            3           10m

Here, DESIRED means how many nodes the DaemonSet wants to run Pods on, CURRENT means how many DaemonSet Pods currently exist, READY means how many are ready, and AVAILABLE shows how many are available to serve their purpose.

For example:
3 eligible nodes
      ↓
DaemonSet
 ┌────┼────┐
 ↓    ↓    ↓
Pod  Pod  Pod
N1   N2   N3

If a new eligible node joins the cluster:
4 eligible nodes
      ↓
DaemonSet
      ↓
4 Pods

Easy way to remember:
DaemonSet = "Run one copy of this Pod on every eligible node."
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe daemonset log-:
This command is used to show detailed information about the log-agent DaemonSet in the drill namespace. It helps you understand which Pods the DaemonSet manages, how many nodes it should run on, the Pod template, labels, container configuration, update strategy, and any events or errors. For example, if log-agent is designed to run a logging agent on every node, this command helps you check whether Kubernetes successfully created and started the required Pod on each eligible node.

You may see information like:
Name:         log-agent
Namespace:    drill
Desired Number of Nodes Scheduled: 3
Current Number of Nodes Scheduled: 3
Number of Nodes Scheduled with Ready Pods: 3
Selector:     app=log-agent

Here, Desired = 3 means the DaemonSet should have a Pod on 3 eligible nodes, Current = 3 means Pods have been scheduled on 3 nodes, and Ready = 3 means all 3 Pods are currently ready.
Node 1 ──→ log-agent Pod ✅
Node 2 ──→ log-agent Pod ✅
Node 3 ──→ log-agent Pod ✅
             ↑
        DaemonSet

The Events section at the bottom is particularly useful for troubleshooting problems such as Pods failing to schedule, image-pull failures, or other DaemonSet issues.
Easy way to remember:
describe daemonset = Get the detailed status, configuration, node placement, and events of a DaemonSet.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get pods -n drill -l ap:
This command is used to find all Pods with the label app=log-agent in the drill namespace and show detailed information about them. The -l app=log-agent filters the Pods so that only Pods belonging to the log-agent application are shown, while -o wide adds extra information such as the Pod IP, Node where the Pod is running, and other details. This is especially useful for checking a DaemonSet because you can verify whether a log-agent Pod is running on each expected node.

For example:
NAME             READY   STATUS    IP           NODE
log-agent-abc    1/1     Running   10.1.0.5     node-1
log-agent-def    1/1     Running   10.1.0.6     node-2
log-agent-ghi    1/1     Running   10.1.0.7     node-3

The flow is:
-l app=log-agent
        ↓
Find Pods with this label
        ↓
-o wide
        ↓
Show extra details
        ↓
Pod → IP → Node

For a DaemonSet:
node-1 → log-agent Pod ✅
node-2 → log-agent Pod ✅
node-3 → log-agent Pod ✅

Easy way to remember:
-l = filter by label
-o wide = show extra Pod details, especially IP and Node.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl rollout status daemonse:
This command is used to check the progress of a DaemonSet rollout named log-agent in the drill namespace. When you update a DaemonSet—for example, changing its container image—Kubernetes gradually updates the Pods running on the eligible nodes. This command lets you watch whether the new Pods have been successfully updated and become ready. For example, if the DaemonSet should run on 3 nodes, Kubernetes will update the Pods and the command will wait until the required Pods are successfully updated and ready.

Example:
Waiting for daemon set "log-agent" rollout to finish:
1 of 3 updated
2 of 3 updated
3 of 3 updated
daemon set "log-agent" successfully rolled out

The flow is:
DaemonSet updated
      ↓
Pods updated one by one
      ↓
Pods become Ready
      ↓
All eligible nodes updated
      ↓
Rollout successful ✅

Easy way to remember:
rollout status daemonset = Check whether the DaemonSet's latest update has successfully rolled out to its Pods/nodes.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl delete daemonset log-ag:
This command is used to delete the log-agent DaemonSet from the drill namespace. When the DaemonSet is deleted, Kubernetes also removes the Pods that were created and managed by that DaemonSet, so the log-agent Pods running on the nodes will normally be terminated as part of the deletion. It does not delete the nodes themselves or other unrelated Deployments, Services, or Pods.

kubectl delete daemonset log-agent -n drill

For example, before deletion:

DaemonSet: log-agent
       ↓
 ┌─────┼─────┐
 ↓     ↓     ↓
Pod   Pod   Pod
N1    N2    N3

After deletion:

DaemonSet: log-agent ❌
       ↓
Pods managed by it ❌

The nodes remain:
Node 1 ✅
Node 2 ✅
Node 3 ✅

Easy way to remember:
delete daemonset = Delete the DaemonSet and the Pods it manages, but keep the Kubernetes nodes themselves.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get statefulset -n dril:
This command is used to list all StatefulSets in the drill namespace and see their basic status. A StatefulSet is used for applications that need stable identity, stable network names, and/or persistent storage, such as databases, Kafka, or other stateful applications. Unlike a normal Deployment, StatefulSet Pods have predictable names such as db-0, db-1, and db-2.

Example output:
NAME   READY   AGE
db     3/3     10m
Here, db is the StatefulSet name, and 3/3 means 3 StatefulSet Pods are expected and all 3 are ready.

For example:
StatefulSet: db
      ↓
 ┌────┼────┐
 ↓    ↓    ↓
db-0 db-1 db-2

Each Pod gets a stable identity:
db-0 → first Pod
db-1 → second Pod
db-2 → third Pod

And if persistent storage is configured, each Pod can have its own storage:
db-0 → PVC → Storage
db-1 → PVC → Storage
db-2 → PVC → Storage

Easy way to remember:
kubectl get statefulset = Check the StatefulSets and their ready Pod count in a namespace.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl describe statefulset we:
This command is used to show detailed information about the web-db StatefulSet in the drill namespace. It helps you understand how the StatefulSet is configured, including how many replicas it should run, which container image it uses, its Pod selector, update strategy, Pod template, storage configuration, and events. For example, if web-db is configured with 3 replicas, Kubernetes creates Pods with stable names such as web-db-0, web-db-1, and web-db-2.

You may see information like:

Name:         web-db
Namespace:    drill
Replicas:     3 desired | 3 total
Selector:     app=web-db
Service Name: web-db

The StatefulSet manages Pods with stable identities:

StatefulSet: web-db
       ↓
 ┌─────┼─────┐
 ↓     ↓     ↓
web-db-0  web-db-1  web-db-2
If persistent storage is configured, each Pod can also have its own persistent volume:

web-db-0 → PVC → Storage
web-db-1 → PVC → Storage
web-db-2 → PVC → Storage

The Events section at the bottom is particularly useful for troubleshooting issues such as Pods failing to start, storage problems, image-pull failures, or scheduling problems.
Easy way to remember:
describe statefulset = See the detailed configuration, Pod identity, replicas, storage, update strategy, and events of a StatefulSet.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl scale statefulset web-d:
This command is used to change the desired number of Pods managed by the web-db StatefulSet to 3 in the drill namespace. Here, web-db is the StatefulSet name and --replicas=3 tells Kubernetes that you want three StatefulSet Pods. Because StatefulSets provide stable Pod identities, Kubernetes creates or maintains Pods with predictable names such as web-db-0, web-db-1, and web-db-2. If there are currently fewer than 3 Pods, Kubernetes creates the missing ones; if there are more than 3, it removes the extra ones according to StatefulSet behavio

For example, if currently there is only:
web-db-0

after scaling:
web-db-0
web-db-1
web-db-2

The flow is:
StatefulSet: web-db
       ↓
--replicas=3
       ↓
3 Pods desired
       ↓
web-db-0
web-db-1
web-db-2

Easy way to remember:
scale statefulset = Change how many Pods a StatefulSet should maintain.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl rollout status stateful:
This command is used to check the progress of a StatefulSet rollout for web-db in the drill namespace. When the StatefulSet is updated, for example by changing its container image or configuration, Kubernetes updates the Pods according to the StatefulSet's update strategy. This command lets you check whether the updated Pods have been successfully created and become ready. For example, if web-db has 3 replicas, Kubernetes may update web-db-0, web-db-1, and web-db-2 in order, depending on the update strategy.

For example:
Waiting for statefulset "web-db" rollout to finish:
1 of 3 updated
2 of 3 updated
3 of 3 updated
statefulset "web-db" successfully rolled out

The flow is:
StatefulSet: web-db
       ↓
New configuration
       ↓
Pods updated
       ↓
web-db-0
       ↓
web-db-1
       ↓
web-db-2
       ↓
All Ready ✅

Easy way to remember:
rollout status statefulset = Check whether the StatefulSet's latest update has successfully rolled out and its Pods are ready.
refEdits.kubectl::kubectl get pvc -n drill -l app:
This command is used to list the PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) in the drill namespace that have the label app=web-db. The -l app=web-db part acts as a filter, so Kubernetes shows only PVCs matching that label. This is especially useful with a StatefulSet because each StatefulSet Pod can have its own PVC for persistent storage. For example, if web-db has 3 replicas, you might see separate PVCs associated with web-db-0, web-db-1, and web-db-2.

For example:

NAME             STATUS   VOLUME       CAPACITY
